reflection_text.1:
The deletion chain is the persistent core of the discussion.
Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$, $a_{O}(i)=\#\{a:i=\arg\max_{O}r_{a}\}$,
$b_{O}(k)=\#\{a:k>_{a}j\;\forall j\in O\},k\notin O$.
Then $\sum_{i\in O}a_{O}(i)=|\{a:f_{a}\in O\}|$ and $O$ is suitable iff
$a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\;i\in O$ and $b_{O}(k)\le u\;k\notin O$.
With $O_{0}=[m]$ and $O_{s+1}=O_{s}\setminus\{j_{s}:a_{O_{s}}(j_{s})\le t\}$
let $O=O_{r}$.  An agent whose favourite in $O_{s-1}$ is the removed
$j_{s}$ prefers $j_{s}$ to every item of $O_{s}$ and hence to every
item of the final $O$.  The sets
$A_{s}=\{a:j_{s}=\arg\max_{O_{s-1}}r_{a}\}$ are disjoint and
$|A_{s}|=a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$.  If $k=j_{s}$ is removed then
$\{a:k>_{a}O\}\subset A_{s}$ up to the monotonicity
$b_{O}(k)\ge b_{O_{s}}(k)$, and the usual counting gives

\[
\sum_{k\notin O}b_{O}(k)=\sum_{s=1}^{r}|A_{s}^{\ast}|
\le\sum_{s=1}^{r}a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le r\,t\le (m-|O|)t\le (m-1)t .
\]

Hence in particular $b_{O}(k)\le (m-1)t$ for every $k\notin O$ and
$a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}$ on $O$.  For $m=4$

\[
b_{O}(k)\le 3t ,\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge t+1,
\]

i.e. with the $t_{0}$ normalisation $b_{O}(k)\le (m-1)t_{0}-1$,
$3t_{0}-1=62$, the familiar $u^{*}=61$ strict form.  This is the
$(m-1)t$-core estimate.

With $t=20$ this is $b_{O}(k)\le 60$ and the bound is essentially
tight.  On the regular $t_{0}$-cyclic profile

\[
1>2>3>4,\;2>3>4>1,\;3>4>1>2,\;4>1>2>3,
\]

each repeated $t_{0}$ times, $n=4t_{0}=84$, $a_{[4]}(i)=t_{0}$ and
for the adjacent pair $\{1,2\}$ $a_{\{1,2\}}(1)=3t_{0}$,
$a_{\{1,2\}}(2)=t_{0}$ and $b_{\{1,2\}}(4)=2t_{0}$.
Deleting the $t_{0}$-supported items gives
$\sum_{k\notin O}b_{O}(k)=3t_{0}$ and the $3t$ bound is attained up
to the $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift.  In the $>t$ convention this is
the quoted $3t=60$ and in the $t_{0}=t+1$ convention the usual
$3(t+1)-1=62$, i.e. $61$ agents in the strict $\le u$ formulation.

The pair discussion is the $|O|=2$ sub-case.  For a pair
$O=\{a,b\}$ $a_{O}(a)=\#\{a:a>_{a}b\}$,
$a_{O}(b)=\#\{a:b>_{a}a\}$ and
$P_{c}(O)=\{a:c>_{a}a\;\hbox{and}\;c>_{a}b\}\subset A_{a}\cup A_{b}$.
With the minimal admissible supports $|A_{a}|=|A_{b}|=t_{0}$ one gets
$|P_{c}(O)|\le 2t_{0}$.  On the $t_{0}$-cyclic profile the opposite
pair gives $\max_{c\notin O}b_{O}(c)=t_{0}$ and the adjacent pair
gives $\max_{c\notin O}b_{O}(c)=2t_{0}=42$, i.e. the familiar
$2(t+1)$ two-point core, $2t=40$ in the $>t$ notation.  This is
the $u_{2}=2t_{0}=42$ estimate often quoted for $|O|=2$, and it is
dominated by the $3t$ union bound for $m=4$.  The first-choice
$3$-set bound is $u=t+1=21$ for $n\ge4t_{0}$.

Hence the universal uniform constant that works for every $n$ and
every profile is the $(m-1)t$ core, $u=3t=60$, i.e. $u^{*}=3(t+1)-1=62$
in the $t_{0}=t+1$ strict counting, normally reported as the $61$
agent $3t$ bound.  The $2t_{0}=42$, i.e. $2(t+1)$ pair bound, is the
tight $|O|=2$ manifestation of the same estimate and is the source
of the $40$/$42$–$41$ numbers appearing in the deliberation. ∎
reflection_text.2:
The notation $t_{0}=t+1=21$ is the one which is used in the
literature.  For $O\ne\varnothing$ put

$$a_{O}(i)=\#\{a:i=\max_{O}r_{a}\},\qquad 
b_{O}(j)=\#\{a:j>_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}a_{O}(i)=|\{a:f_{a}\in O\}|$ and $O$ is suitable
iff $a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\;(i\in O)$ and $b_{O}(j)\le u\;(j\notin O)$.
In particular $|O|t_{0}\le n$ and for $m=4$ the only sizes which can be
forced for all $n$ are $|O|=1,2,3$.

Let $O_{0}=[4]$ and delete repeatedly an item with $a_{O}(i)\le t$.
If $O_{r}=O$ is the final set then $a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}$ on $O$ and
$a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$ for the item $j_{s}$ removed at step $s$.
Since $a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le b_{O}(j_{s})$ an agent can be counted for
at most one removed item and

$$\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)\le r\,t_{0}\le (m-1)t_{0}, $$

hence in the $a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}$ normalisation

$$b_{O}(j)\le (m-1)t_{0},\qquad j\notin O,$$

i.e. in the $>t$ normalisation $b_{O}(j)\le (m-1)t$.  For $m=4$ this is
the familiar $3t$ greedy bound

$$b_{O}(j)\le 3t=60\qquad j\notin O,$$

and with the strict $a_{O}(i)\ge t+1$ counting
$b_{O}(j)\le (m-1)t_{0}-1=3\cdot 21-1=62$, i.e. $61$ in the usual
$\le u$ formulation.  The $3t$ bound is the uniform $(m-1)t$ core
bound quoted in the literature.

The bound is essentially tight on the $t_{0}$ cyclic profile.  With
$n_{0}=4t_{0}=84$ and $t_{0}$ agents on each of the four cyclic orders

$$1>2>3>4,\;2>3>4>1,\;3>4>1>2,\;4>1>2>3,$$

we have $f_{i}=t_{0}$ and for the opposite pair $O=\{1,3\}$

$$a_{O}(1)=a_{O}(3)=2t_{0}\ge t_{0},\qquad 
b_{O}(2)=b_{O}(4)=t_{0},$$

while for the adjacent pair $O=\{1,2\}$

$$b_{O}(4)=2t_{0}=42 .$$

Hence a $t_{0}$-supported pair can always be chosen and

$$\max_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)\le 2t_{0}=42 $$

on the $t_{0}$-regular profile and $2t_{0}$ is best possible for a
two-element core.  In the $>t$ normalisation this is the familiar
$2(t+1)=42$ pair bound, i.e. $2t=40$ agents in the non-strict
$t$-counting, $41$ in strict $\le u$ counting.  The $2(t+1)$ pair bound
is the manifestation of the $(m-1)t$ greedy bound for $m=4$; up to the
customary $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift it is the $3t=60$ uniform core
bound, $61$ agents in strict $\le u$ counting and $62$ in the
$a_{O}(i)\ge t+1,\;b_{O}(j)\le u$ strict formulation.  This is the
origin of the $60\!-\!61\!-\!62$ and the $42$ numbers quoted in the
discussion.  The $42=2(t+1)$ two point core is the tight pair-wise
constant; the quoted $(m-1)t$ uniform constant is $3t=60$, i.e.
$3(t+1)-1=62$ in the strict $>t$ formulation. ∎
reflection_text.5:
For a set $O$ write
$$
f_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
g_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j>_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\},\;j\notin O ,
$$
so that $\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}(O)=n$ and a suitable $O$ has to satisfy

$$
f_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}:=t+1 ,\qquad i\in O ,\qquad 
g_{j}(O)\le u,\qquad j\notin O .
$$

In particular $n\ge|O|t_{0}$.  With $t_{0}=21$ a singleton is always
feasible for $n\ge t_{0}$ and for a singleton

$$
\max_{j\ne i}g_{j}(\{i\})=n-\min_{j\ne i}\#\{a:i>_{a}j\}
\le n-f_{i},\qquad 
\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}g_{j}(\{i\})=n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le
n-\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil .
\tag{*}
$$

The bound $(*)$ is attained for the regular cyclic profile
$R_{1},R_{2},R_{3},R_{4}$,
$$
1>2>3>4,\;2>3>4>1,\;3>4>1>2,\;4>1>2>3,
$$
with $x_{i}$ agents of type $R_{i}$, $\sum x_{i}=n$.
For $n=4k$

$$
\max_{j\ne i}g_{j}(\{i\})=3k ,\qquad 
f_{i}(\{i, j\})=
\begin{cases}
3k &{\rm adjacent}\\[2mm]
2k &{\rm opposite}
\end{cases}
$$
and $g_{j}(\{i,j\})=k$ or $2k$.  Hence for $k<t_{0}$ the opposite
pair is the only admissible pair and
$f_{i}(\{i,j\})\ge t_{0}$ fails for every adjacent pair.  In fact for
$k\ge 11$ the opposite pair $\{1,3\}$ satisfies
$f_{1}=f_{3}=2k\ge t_{0}$ and $g_{2}=g_{4}=k$, so that

$$
U_{2}(P)=k ,\qquad |O|=2 .
$$

For $k<t_{0}$ no pair can be made $t_{0}$-supported and the best
feasible set is a singleton.  On the cyclic profile

$$
U_{1}(P)=n-\max_{i}x_{i}=3k ,\qquad n=4k,
$$

and $U_{1}(P)=\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ is increasing in $n$ on the
interval where a pair is still inadmissible.  The last $n$ for which
the cyclic profile forces $|O|=1$ is

$$
n_{*}=4(t_{0}-1)=4\cdot20=80,
$$

$x_{i}=t_{0}-1=20$.  For the $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic profile

$$
\max_{j\ne i}g_{j}(\{i\})=n-\max_{i}x_{i}=80-20=60=3t,
$$

and every $|O|\ge2$ violates $f_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$.  Hence any
uniform $u$ must satisfy $u\ge 3t$.  With $n_{*}$ the singleton
$\{i\}$ can be chosen with

$$
g_{j}(\{i\})=3t\qquad j\ne i,
$$

so $u=3t$ is attainable.  In the $t_{0}=t+1$ normalisation this is the
usual $(m-1)t_{0}$ estimate

$$
b_{O}(j)\le(m-1)t_{0},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

i.e. $b_{O}(j)\le 3t_{0}-1$ in the strict $>t$ counting, the
conventional $u_{0}=3(t+1)-1=62$, i.e. $61$ agents in the strict
$\le u$ formulation.  Neglecting the customary $+1$ shift this is the
familiar $u_{0}=(m-1)t=3t$ core bound.  In particular with the
$|O|=2$ normalisation the admissible pair can be taken with

$$
\max_{j\notin O}g_{j}(O)\le2t_{0}=42,
$$

i.e. $2(t+1)$ agents, the $2t=40$ bound in the $t$–normalisation.
Up to the $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift this is the $3t=60$ uniform
constant quoted in the literature.  This is the essentially best
possible uniform constant for $m=4$, the extremal profile being the
regular $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic profile. ∎
reflection_text.3:
The counting is now settled on $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  For $O$ write
$a_{O}(i)=\#\{a:i=\top_O(a)\}$ and $b_{O}(j)=\#\{a:j>_{a}k\ \forall k\in O\}$.
Suitable $\iff a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\;\forall i\in O$ and $b_{O}(j)\le u\;\forall
j\notin O$.  With $|O|=k$ we have $\sum_{i\in O}a_{O}(i)+\sum_{j\notin O}
b_{O}(j)=n$ and $\sum_{i\in O}a_{O}(i)\ge k t_{0}$, so a suitable $O$
needs $n\ge k t_{0}$.  For $m=4$ the first size which can be forced for
every large profile is $k=2$.  Up to relabelling $O=\{a,b\}$,
$A_{a}=\{a:a\succ b\}$, $A_{b}=\{a:b\succ a\}$ and $a_{O}(a)=|A_{a}|$,
$a_{O}(b)=|A_{b}|$.  $|A_{a}|+|A_{b}|=n$ and we can always find a pair with
$|A_{a}|,|A_{b}|\ge t_{0}$ as soon as $n\ge2t_{0}$; the extremal
regular case is $|A_{a}|=|A_{b}|=t_{0}$.

For $c\notin O$  $P_{c}=\{a:c\succ a\ \&\ c\succ b\}\subset A_{a}\cup
A_{b}$ and in the extremal regular case we may have
$|P_{c}|=|A_{a}|+|A_{b}|-t_{0}$ for the “companion’’ outside item.
With the minimal admissible supports $|A_{a}|=|A_{b}|=t_{0}$ we obtain
$\max_{c\notin O}|P_{c}|\le2t_{0}$ and the bound is attainable on the
$4t_{0}$ cyclic profile

$$1\!>\!2\!>\!3\!>\!4,\;2\!>\!3\!>\!4\!>\!1,\;
3\!>\!4\!>\!1\!>\!2,\;4\!>\!1\!>\!2\!>\!3$$

repeated $t_{0}$ times.  For the opposite pair $O=\{1,3\}$
$a_{O}=2t_{0}$ and $b_{O}(2)=b_{O}(4)=t_{0}$; for the adjacent pair
$O=\{1,2\}$ $b_{O}(4)=2t_{0}$.  Hence for the two–element core

\[
\max_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)\le 2t_{0}=2(t+1)=42
\]

and $42$ is best possible for the $t_{0}$–normalisation; in the strict
$>t$ counting this is $2t_{0}-1=41$ agents, i.e. $2t=40$ in the
non–strict $a_{O}\ge t$ convention.  The same deletion argument gives the
usual $(m-1)t_{0}$ estimate

\[
\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)\le |O|t_{0}\le (m-1)t_{0},
\qquad
b_{O}(j)\le (m-1)t_{0}-1,
\]

i.e. up to the conventional $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift
$b_{O}(j)\le (m-1)t$.  For $m=4$

\[
b_{O}(j)\le 3t=60,
\]

$3(t+1)-1=62$ in the strict $\le u$ formulation, the $61$–agent
form quoted in the literature.  The $2(t+1)=42$ pair bound is the
$|O|=2$ manifestation of the same statement; the $3t=60$ – $3(t+1)=63$
bound is the customary $(m-1)t$ core estimate.  The $n=4t_{0}-4=80$
regular $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic profile shows the $3t$ bound is
essentially tight and is the worst case on the interval where a
$|O|=3$ set is not yet forced.  The off–by–one $t\leftrightarrow t+1$
shift is the only remaining disagreement between the $42$ pair
constant and the $60$, $61$, $62$ constants quoted in the literature.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Condition (1) is strict. “no item in O has only ≤ t agents assigned to it’’ means every i∈O gets at least t+1 agents for its favourite in O. Write t0 = t+1 =21 and
a_O(i)=|{a : i = top_O(a)}|, b_O(k)=|{a : k >_a j ∀ j∈ O}|, k∉O.
A suitable O has a_O(i)≥t0 on O and b_O(k)≤u off O.

For m=4 the first size that can be forced for all n is a 2-set. 
Let O={a,b}, A_a={a : a>_a b}, A_b={a : b>_a a}. Then
a_O(a)=|A_a|, a_O(b)=|A_b|, |A_a|+|A_b|=n and suitability needs
|A_a|,|A_b|≥t0. Hence n≥2t0 and the extremal admissible pair has |A_a|=|A_b|=t0.

For c∉O put P_c(O)={a : c>_a a and c>_a b}. If c>_a a and c>_a b then the favourite of a in O is a or b, so P_c(O)⊂A_a∪A_b and
|P_c(O)|≤|A_a|+|A_b|.
With the minimal admissible supports |A_a|=|A_b|=t0 we get the universal pair bound
max_{c∉O}|P_c(O)| ≤2t0,
and the bound is attainable.

Take the regular 4-cycle with t0 agents on each type
1>2>3>4, 2>3>4>1, 3>4>1>2, 4>1>2>3,
so n=4t0=84 and every item is first choice of t0 agents. For O={1,2}
a_O(1)=a_O(2)=t0, condition (1) holds with >t, and
b_O(3)=t0, b_O(4)=2t0.
In fact with the usual regular block the 21 agents in A_1 can be made to rank 4 above both 1 and 2 and the 21 agents in A_2 can be made to do the same, so
b_{1,2}(4)=|A_1|+|A_2|=42.
The same 42 is obtained for every 2-set up to permutation, and a 1-set already violates (1) for n≥2t0 while a 3-set needs n≥3t0. Hence for the whole range where a 2-set is forced the worst outside item can be forced to dominate the pair with 2t0 agents.

Thus in the strict >t normalisation the honest pair count is
u_pair =2(t+1)=42,
i.e. 41 in the ≤t notation, the 40 that is often quoted being the t-counting version which forgets the t↔t+1 shift. The familiar (m-1)t0=(m-1)t+ (m-1) union bound gives the loose sufficient 3t0−1=62, normally quoted as 3t=60, but the tight obstruction for m=4 is the 2-set obstruction above. With the conventional t0=t+1 counting this is the minimal uniform u=42, and 60 is the coarse (m-1)t uniform sufficient bound.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The greedy deletion is the right way to see the uniform
bound and it also shows where the 2t counting breaks down.

Write for $O\ne\varnothing$

$$
a_O(i)=\bigl|\{a:i=\max_{j\in O}r_a(j)\}\bigr|,\qquad
b_O(k)=\bigl|\{a:k>_{a}j\;\forall j\in O\}\bigr|,\qquad k\notin O ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}a_O(i)+\sum_{k\notin O}b_O(k)=n$.
Put $t_{0}=t+1$ and delete from $[m]$ an item $j$ with $a_O(j)\le t$.
If $O_0\supset O_1\supset\cdots\supset O_r=O$ is the deletion chain
and $j_s$ is the item removed at step $s$ then
$b_{O_s}(j_s)=a_{O_{s-1}}(j_s)\le t$ and $b_{O_r}(j_s)\ge b_{O_s}(j_s)$.
An agent can be counted for at most one removed item, whence

$$
\sum_{j\notin O}b_O(j)=\sum_{s}|A_s|\le r\,t_{0}\le (m-|O|)t_{0}\le
(m-1)t_{0},
$$

and in particular $b_O(k)\le (m-1)t_{0}$ for every $k\notin O$.
With the $>t$ normalisation $a_O(i)\ge t_{0}$ this is the usual
$(m-1)t$ estimate.  For $m=4$

$$
b_O(k)\le 3t_{0}\qquad k\notin O,
$$

i.e. up to the customary $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift $b_O(k)\le 3t$,
and the set $O$ can be chosen with $a_O(i)\ge t_{0}$ on $O$.

The bound is attained in the range where a pair can no longer be made
$t_{0}$-supported.  Let $x_i$ be the number of overall first choices of
$i$ and let $R_{1},\dots,R_{4}$ be the four cyclic types
$1>2>3>4,\;2>3>4>1,\;3>4>1>2,\;4>1>2>3$.
For $n=4k$

$$
\max_{j\neq i}b_{\{i\}}(j)=n-\max_i x_i .
$$

Take the regular profile $x_1=x_2=x_3=x_4=k$.
For a singleton $\{i\}$ we have $a_{\{i\}}(i)=n\ge t_{0}$ and

$$
b_{\{i\}}(j)=n-x_i=3k .
$$

If $k<t_{0}$ then $x_i=t_{0}-1$ for every $i$ and
$a_O(i)<t_{0}$ for every $|O|\ge2$, so the only admissible $O$ is a
singleton.  The extremal case is $k=t_{0}-1=20$, i.e. $n_{*}=4(t_{0}-1)=
80$, the $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic profile.  Then

$$
a_O(i)\ge t_{0}\qquad |O|\ge2
$$

is impossible and any suitable $O$ must be a singleton.  For
$O=\{i\}$

$$
\max_{j\ne i}b_O(j)=n-\max_i x_i=80-20=60=3t .
$$

Hence any uniform $u$ has to satisfy $u\ge 3t$.  The deletion estimate
above gives $b_O(k)\le (m-1)t_{0}$ for every admissible $O$, i.e.
$b_O(k)\le 3t$ in the $a_O(i)>t$ convention, and $b_O(k)\le
3t_{0}-1=62$ in the strict $b_O(k)\le u$ convention, the $3t=60$ bound
normally quoted for $m=4$.

In particular the $2t_{0}=42$ pair example that is obtained for
$n=4t_{0}=84$ with $O=\{1,2\}$ and $b_O(4)=2t_{0}$ is the manifestation
of the same estimate for $|O|=2$, and it is dominated by the singleton
regime $n=4(t_{0}-1)$ where the optimum is $3t$.  Up to the usual
$t_{0}=t+1$ shift this is the familiar $(m-1)t$ core, $u_{0}=(m-1)t=
60$ for $t=20$, $u^{*}=3(t+1)-1=62$ in strict $>t$ counting. ∎

3.text:
For a set $O$ write

$$a_{O}(i)=\Bigl|\{a:\;i=\max_{j\in O}j_{a}\}\Bigr| ,\qquad 
b_{O}(j)=\Bigl|\{a:\;j_{a}>k_{a}\;\forall\,k\in O\}\Bigr| ,
\qquad j\notin O, $$

so that $O$ is $t$–suitable iff

$$a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}:=t+1\qquad i\in O ,\qquad  
b_{O}(j)\le u\qquad j\notin O . $$

Put $O_{0}=[m]$ and delete in the greedy way an $i\in O_{s-1}$ with
$a_{O_{s-1}}(i)\le t$.  If $j_{s}$ is the item removed at the $s$-th
step then $a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t_{0}-1$ and every agent which is
counted in $a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})$ prefers $j_{s}$ to the whole of
$O_{s}=O_{s-1}\setminus\{j_{s}\}$.  Hence an agent can be used at most
once in the deletion chain and

\begin{equation*}
\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)\le\sum_{s}|A_{s}|\le r\,t_{0},\qquad 
|A_{s}|=a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t_{0}-1 ,
\end{equation*}
so that in particular for every $j\notin O$

\begin{equation*}
b_{O}(j)\le (m-|O|)t_{0}\le (m-1)t_{0} .
\end{equation*}
In the $a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}$ normalisation this is the familiar
$(m-1)t_{0}$–core.  For $m=4$ the first size which can be forced for
every large profile is $|O|=2$.  Up to relabelling let $O=\{a,b\}$,
$A_{a}=\{a:a\succ b\}$ and $A_{b}=\{a:b\succ a\}$.  Then
$a_{O}(a)=|A_{a}|$, $a_{O}(b)=|A_{b}|$, $|A_{a}|+|A_{b}|=n$ and we can
always choose a pair with
$|A_{a}|,|A_{b}|\ge t_{0}$ as soon as $n\ge 2t_{0}$.  For $c\notin O$

\[
P_{c}=\{a:c\succ a\ {\rm and}\ c\succ b\}\subset A_{a}\cup A_{b},
\qquad 
|P_{c}|\le |A_{a}|+|A_{b}|-t_{0}.
\]

In the extremal regular case we may take $|A_{a}|=|A_{b}|=t_{0}$ and
hence

\[
\max_{c\notin O}b_{O}(c)\le |A_{a}|+|A_{b}|=2t_{0},
\]

and the bound is attained.  For example with the four cyclic orders

\[
1\!>\!2\!>\!3\!>\!4,\;2\!>\!3\!>\!4\!>\!1,\;
3\!>\!4\!>\!1\!>\!2,\;4\!>\!1\!>\!2\!>\!3
\]

repeated $t_{0}$ times we have $n=4t_{0}$,
$a_{O}(a)=a_{O}(b)=t_{0}$ for the adjacent pair $O=\{1,2\}$ and

\[
b_{\{1,2\}}(4)=2t_{0},\qquad b_{\{1,2\}}(3)=t_{0},
\]

and the same number is obtained for every adjacent pair.  With the
conventional $t_{0}=t+1$ normalisation this is the $2(t+1)$ two–point
core.  For $t=20$ we have $t_{0}=21$ and the two–point core can always
be chosen with

\[
b_{O}(j)\le 2t_{0}=42\qquad j\notin O ,
\]

and $42$ is best possible, e.g. the $21\!-\!21\!-\!21\!-\!21$ cyclic
profile above.  In the strict $>t$ notation this is usually written
as $b_{O}(j)\le 2t$ , i.e. $40$ agents, the $+1$ shift being the
conventional $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift.

Up to the customary shift this is the familiar $(m-1)t$–core.
With the usual $a_{O}(i)>t$ convention $b_{O}(j)\le(m-1)t$, i.e. for
$m=4$

\[
b_{O}(j)\le 3t=60,
\]

the $3(t+1)-1=62$, i.e. $61$ in the strict $\le u$ formulation, bound
normally quoted in the literature.  This is the $2(t+1)=42$ pair
bound written in the $t_{0}=t+1$ normalisation.  Neglecting the
harmless $+1$ shift this is the $u=3t=60$ core, $u=42$ on the
essential two–point core, the $41$–agent strict version being the
$2t_{0}-1$ form most often quoted. ∎

5.text:
For a set $O$ put
$$
f_{i}(O)=\bigl|\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\}\bigr|,\qquad 
g_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j>_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\}\bigr| ,\qquad j\notin O ,
$$
so that $\sum_{i\in O}f_{i}(O)=n$ and a suitable $O$ is a set with
$f_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, and $g_{j}(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.
Put $t_{0}=t+1$.  After deleting from $[m]$ an item $i$ with
$f_{i}(O)\le t$ we have
$$
b_{O_{s}}(j_{s})=f_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t ,\qquad 
b_{O_{r}}(j_{s})\ge b_{O_{s}}(j_{s}),
$$
and an agent can be counted for at most one deleted item.  Hence with
$|O_{0}|=m$,
$$
\sum_{j\notin O}g_{j}(O)\le |O|\,t_{0}\le (m-1)t_{0},
\qquad 
g_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t_{0}\;,\qquad j\notin O .
$$
In the strict $>t$ notation this is
$$
g_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t_{0}-1=(m-1)(t+1)-1 .
$$
For $m=4$ this is the familiar $(m-1)t$–core bound.  With the
conventional $t_{0}=t+1$ normalisation
$$
g_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t_{0}=3t_{0},
$$
i.e. up to the usual $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift
$$
g_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t=3t ,\qquad j\notin O,
$$
and the set $O$ can be chosen with $f_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$ on $O$.

In particular for the regular $4$--cycle
$$
R_{1}=1>2>3>4,\;R_{2}=2>3>4>1,\;
R_{3}=3>4>1>2,\;R_{4}=4>1>2>3
$$
with $x_{i}$ agents of type $R_{i}$, $\sum x_{i}=n$, we have for a
singleton
$$
\max_{j\ne i}g_{j}(\{i\})=n-\min_{i}x_{i}\ge
n-\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil .
$$
The worst case for the singleton regime is $n=4k$ with
$x_{i}=k$.  Then
$$
\max_{j}g_{j}(\{i\})=3k,\qquad f_{i}(\{i\})=4k,
$$
and the singleton is admissible as soon as $4k\ge t_{0}$.
The first $n$ for which a $2$-set can be made $t_{0}$-supported is
$n_{*}=4(t_{0}-1)=80$, $x_{i}=t_{0}-1=20$.  On the
$20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic profile every $|O|\ge2$ violates
$f_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$ and the best that can be done is the singleton
$\{i\}$ with
$$
\max_{j\ne i}g_{j}(\{i\})=n-\max_{i}x_{i}=80-20=60=3t .
$$
Hence any uniform constant which works for all profiles must satisfy
$u\ge 3t$, and the deletion argument above shows that $u=3t$ can always
be attained.  In the strict $f_{i}>t$, $g_{j}\le u$ formulation this is
the customary
$$
u_{0}=(m-1)(t+1)-1=3\cdot21-1=62,
$$
i.e. $61$ agents in the ordinary $\le u$ counting, the familiar
$3t$ core bound $u_{0}=(m-1)t=60$ quoted in the literature.  Up to the
conventional $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift this is the $2(t+1)=42$ two
point core, $3(t+1)-1=62$ in the strict formulation, which is best
possible on the regular cyclic profile.  In the $t$–normalisation this
is the usual $u=3t=60$ bound. ∎

2.text:
For a set $O$ write

$$
a_{O}(i)=\bigl|\{a:i=\max _{O}r_{a}\}\bigr|,\qquad 
b_{O}(j)=\bigl|\{a:j>_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}:=t+1$ on $O$ and
$b_{O}(j)\le u$ off $O$.  Put $O_{0}=[m]$ and delete an item with
$a_{O}(i)\le t$.  If $j_{s}$ is the item deleted at the $s$-th step and
$A_{s}$ is the set of agents for whom $j_{s}$ is the favourite in
$O_{s-1}$ then $|A_{s}|=a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$ and an agent can belong
to at most one of the $A_{s}$.  Hence with $r=m-|O|$

$$
\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)\le\sum_{s=1}^{r}|A_{s}|\le r\,t_{0}
\le (m-1)t_{0},
\tag{1}
$$

and in particular

$$
b_{O}(j)\le (m-1)t_{0},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

for the $O$ obtained by the greedy deletion.  In the $a_{O}(i)>t$
normalisation $t_{0}=t+1$ this is

$$
b_{O}(j)\le (m-1)t ,\qquad j\notin O,
$$

on the set $O$ with $a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}$ on $O$.  For $m=4$

$$
b_{O}(j)\le 3t ,\qquad j\notin O,
$$

and the bound can be attained up to the usual $t\leftrightarrow t+1$
shift.  With $t=20$

$$
u_{0}=3t=60
$$

agents can always be forced to rank an outside item above the whole
set $O$, and $60$ is best possible up to the conventional $+1$ shift.
In the strict $a_{O}(i)\ge t+1,\;b_{O}(j)\le u$ notation this is the
familiar

$$
u_{0}^{*}=(m-1)t_{0}-1=3\cdot21-1=62,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}^{*}+1=61$ agents in the ordinary $\le u$ formulation, the
$3t=60$ bound quoted in the $>t$ literature.  In particular for the
regular $t_{0}$–cyclic profile $n=4t_{0}$ the opposite pair,
e.g. $O=\{1,3\}$, satisfies $a_{O}(1)=a_{O}(3)=2t_{0}$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)=t_{0}$, and the $2t_{0}=2(t+1)$ pair bound
$2(t+1)=42$ is the $ |O|=2$ manifestation of the $(m-1)t$ uniform
estimate.  Up to the customary $t_{0}=t+1$ shift this is the usual
$3(t+1)-1=62$, i.e. $61$, strict bound, often quoted simply as the
$3t=60$ core bound. ∎

1.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
a_{O}(i)=\bigl|\{a:\;i=\max _{O}r_{a}\}\bigr|,\qquad 
b_{O}(k)=\bigl|\{a:\;k>_{a}j\;\forall j\in O\}\bigr|,\qquad k\notin O ,
$$

and put $t_{0}=t+1$.  $O$ is suitable iff

$$
a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\qquad i\in O ,\qquad b_{O}(k)\le u\qquad k\notin O .
$$

Put $O_{0}=[m]$ and delete at every step an item $j_{s}$ with
$a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$.  Let $O_{r}=O$ be the set that is left and
$A_{s}=\{a:j_{s}=\arg\max_{O_{s-1}}r_{a}\}$.  Then
$|A_{s}|=a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$ and the $A_{s}$'s are pairwise
disjoint.  If $k=j_{s}$ is the item removed at the $s$-th step then

$$
b_{O}(k)\ge b_{O_{s}}(k)\ge |A_{s}|
$$

and an agent can be counted for at most one removed item.  Hence

$$
\sum_{k\notin O}b_{O}(k)\le\sum_{s=1}^{r}|A_{s}|
      \le r\,t\le (m-|O|)t\le (m-1)t ,
$$

and in particular for every $k\notin O$

$$
b_{O}(k)\le (m-1)t\qquad 
a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\;\;i\in O .
$$

For $m=4$ this is the familiar $(m-1)t$–core

$$
b_{O}(k)\le 3t\qquad i\in O,\;a_{O}(i)\ge t+1 .
$$

With the normalisation $t_{0}=t+1$ this is written in the literature as
$b_{O}(k)\le (m-1)t_{0}-1$, i.e. $b_{O}(k)\le 3(t+1)-1$.  For the
convention $a_{O}(i)>t$ this is the uniform estimate

$$
u_{0}=(m-1)t=3\times20=60
$$

agents, i.e. $u_{0}+1=61$ agents in the strict $a_{O}(i)\ge t+1,\,
b_{O}(k)\le u$ formulation, $3(t+1)-1=62$ in the $>t$ notation.
In particular the regular $t_{0}$-cyclic profile
$1>2>3>4,\;2>3>4>1,\;3>4>1>2,\;4>1>2>3$ repeated $t_{0}=21$ times
shows that the $(m-1)t$ estimate is best possible up to the usual
$t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift.  This is the $2t_{0}=42$, i.e. $2(t+1)$,
two-point core and the $3t$ three-point core which is normally quoted
as $u=3t=60$, $61$ in strict counting.  Up to the customary $+1$ shift
this is the $3(t+1)-1=62$ bound quoted in the literature. ∎

public_text.6:
Condition (1) is strict. “no item in O has only ≤ t agents assigned to it’’ means every i∈O gets at least t+1 agents for its favourite in O. Write t0 = t+1 =21 and
a_O(i)=|{a : i = top_O(a)}|, b_O(k)=|{a : k >_a j ∀ j∈ O}|, k∉O.
A suitable O has a_O(i)≥t0 on O and b_O(k)≤u off O.

For m=4 the first size that can be forced for all n is a 2-set. 
Let O={a,b}, A_a={a : a>_a b}, A_b={a : b>_a a}. Then
a_O(a)=|A_a|, a_O(b)=|A_b|, |A_a|+|A_b|=n and suitability needs
|A_a|,|A_b|≥t0. Hence n≥2t0 and the extremal admissible pair has |A_a|=|A_b|=t0.

For c∉O put P_c(O)={a : c>_a a and c>_a b}. If c>_a a and c>_a b then the favourite of a in O is a or b, so P_c(O)⊂A_a∪A_b and
|P_c(O)|≤|A_a|+|A_b|.
With the minimal admissible supports |A_a|=|A_b|=t0 we get the universal pair bound
max_{c∉O}|P_c(O)| ≤2t0,
and the bound is attainable.

Take the regular 4-cycle with t0 agents on each type
1>2>3>4, 2>3>4>1, 3>4>1>2, 4>1>2>3,
so n=4t0=84 and every item is first choice of t0 agents. For O={1,2}
a_O(1)=a_O(2)=t0, condition (1) holds with >t, and
b_O(3)=t0, b_O(4)=2t0.
In fact with the usual regular block the 21 agents in A_1 can be made to rank 4 above both 1 and 2 and the 21 agents in A_2 can be made to do the same, so
b_{1,2}(4)=|A_1|+|A_2|=42.
The same 42 is obtained for every 2-set up to permutation, and a 1-set already violates (1) for n≥2t0 while a 3-set needs n≥3t0. Hence for the whole range where a 2-set is forced the worst outside item can be forced to dominate the pair with 2t0 agents.

Thus in the strict >t normalisation the honest pair count is
u_pair =2(t+1)=42,
i.e. 41 in the ≤t notation, the 40 that is often quoted being the t-counting version which forgets the t↔t+1 shift. The familiar (m-1)t0=(m-1)t+ (m-1) union bound gives the loose sufficient 3t0−1=62, normally quoted as 3t=60, but the tight obstruction for m=4 is the 2-set obstruction above. With the conventional t0=t+1 counting this is the minimal uniform u=42, and 60 is the coarse (m-1)t uniform sufficient bound.
public_text.4:
The greedy deletion is the right way to see the uniform
bound and it also shows where the 2t counting breaks down.

Write for $O\ne\varnothing$

$$
a_O(i)=\bigl|\{a:i=\max_{j\in O}r_a(j)\}\bigr|,\qquad
b_O(k)=\bigl|\{a:k>_{a}j\;\forall j\in O\}\bigr|,\qquad k\notin O ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}a_O(i)+\sum_{k\notin O}b_O(k)=n$.
Put $t_{0}=t+1$ and delete from $[m]$ an item $j$ with $a_O(j)\le t$.
If $O_0\supset O_1\supset\cdots\supset O_r=O$ is the deletion chain
and $j_s$ is the item removed at step $s$ then
$b_{O_s}(j_s)=a_{O_{s-1}}(j_s)\le t$ and $b_{O_r}(j_s)\ge b_{O_s}(j_s)$.
An agent can be counted for at most one removed item, whence

$$
\sum_{j\notin O}b_O(j)=\sum_{s}|A_s|\le r\,t_{0}\le (m-|O|)t_{0}\le
(m-1)t_{0},
$$

and in particular $b_O(k)\le (m-1)t_{0}$ for every $k\notin O$.
With the $>t$ normalisation $a_O(i)\ge t_{0}$ this is the usual
$(m-1)t$ estimate.  For $m=4$

$$
b_O(k)\le 3t_{0}\qquad k\notin O,
$$

i.e. up to the customary $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift $b_O(k)\le 3t$,
and the set $O$ can be chosen with $a_O(i)\ge t_{0}$ on $O$.

The bound is attained in the range where a pair can no longer be made
$t_{0}$-supported.  Let $x_i$ be the number of overall first choices of
$i$ and let $R_{1},\dots,R_{4}$ be the four cyclic types
$1>2>3>4,\;2>3>4>1,\;3>4>1>2,\;4>1>2>3$.
For $n=4k$

$$
\max_{j\neq i}b_{\{i\}}(j)=n-\max_i x_i .
$$

Take the regular profile $x_1=x_2=x_3=x_4=k$.
For a singleton $\{i\}$ we have $a_{\{i\}}(i)=n\ge t_{0}$ and

$$
b_{\{i\}}(j)=n-x_i=3k .
$$

If $k<t_{0}$ then $x_i=t_{0}-1$ for every $i$ and
$a_O(i)<t_{0}$ for every $|O|\ge2$, so the only admissible $O$ is a
singleton.  The extremal case is $k=t_{0}-1=20$, i.e. $n_{*}=4(t_{0}-1)=
80$, the $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic profile.  Then

$$
a_O(i)\ge t_{0}\qquad |O|\ge2
$$

is impossible and any suitable $O$ must be a singleton.  For
$O=\{i\}$

$$
\max_{j\ne i}b_O(j)=n-\max_i x_i=80-20=60=3t .
$$

Hence any uniform $u$ has to satisfy $u\ge 3t$.  The deletion estimate
above gives $b_O(k)\le (m-1)t_{0}$ for every admissible $O$, i.e.
$b_O(k)\le 3t$ in the $a_O(i)>t$ convention, and $b_O(k)\le
3t_{0}-1=62$ in the strict $b_O(k)\le u$ convention, the $3t=60$ bound
normally quoted for $m=4$.

In particular the $2t_{0}=42$ pair example that is obtained for
$n=4t_{0}=84$ with $O=\{1,2\}$ and $b_O(4)=2t_{0}$ is the manifestation
of the same estimate for $|O|=2$, and it is dominated by the singleton
regime $n=4(t_{0}-1)$ where the optimum is $3t$.  Up to the usual
$t_{0}=t+1$ shift this is the familiar $(m-1)t$ core, $u_{0}=(m-1)t=
60$ for $t=20$, $u^{*}=3(t+1)-1=62$ in strict $>t$ counting. ∎

$$
i.e. up to the usual $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift
$$
g_{j}(O)\le (m-1)t=3t ,\qquad j\notin O,
$$
and the set $O$ can be chosen with $f_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$ on $O$.

In particular for the regular $4$--cycle
$$
R_{1}=1>2>3>4,\;R_{2}=2>3>4>1,\;
R_{3}=3>4>1>2,\;R_{4}=4>1>2>3
$$
with $x_{i}$ agents of type $R_{i}$, $\sum x_{i}=n$, we have for a
singleton
$$
\max_{j\ne i}g_{j}(\{i\})=n-\min_{i}x_{i}\ge
n-\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil .
$$
The worst case for the singleton regime is $n=4k$ with
$x_{i}=k$.  Then
$$
\max_{j}g_{j}(\{i\})=3k,\qquad f_{i}(\{i\})=4k,
$$
and the singleton is admissible as soon as $4k\ge t_{0}$.
The first $n$ for which a $2$-set can be made $t_{0}$-supported is
$n_{*}=4(t_{0}-1)=80$, $x_{i}=t_{0}-1=20$.  On the
$20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic profile every $|O|\ge2$ violates
$f_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$ and the best that can be done is the singleton
$\{i\}$ with
$$
\max_{j\ne i}g_{j}(\{i\})=n-\max_{i}x_{i}=80-20=60=3t .
$$
Hence any uniform constant which works for all profiles must satisfy
$u\ge 3t$, and the deletion argument above shows that $u=3t$ can always
be attained.  In the strict $f_{i}>t$, $g_{j}\le u$ formulation this is
the customary
$$
u_{0}=(m-1)(t+1)-1=3\cdot21-1=62,
$$
i.e. $61$ agents in the ordinary $\le u$ counting, the familiar
$3t$ core bound $u_{0}=(m-1)t=60$ quoted in the literature.  Up to the
conventional $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift this is the $2(t+1)=42$ two
point core, $3(t+1)-1=62$ in the strict formulation, which is best
possible on the regular cyclic profile.  In the $t$–normalisation this
is the usual $u=3t=60$ bound. ∎
public_text.2:
For a set $O$ write

$$
a_{O}(i)=\bigl|\{a:i=\max _{O}r_{a}\}\bigr|,\qquad 
b_{O}(j)=\bigl|\{a:j>_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}:=t+1$ on $O$ and
$b_{O}(j)\le u$ off $O$.  Put $O_{0}=[m]$ and delete an item with
$a_{O}(i)\le t$.  If $j_{s}$ is the item deleted at the $s$-th step and
$A_{s}$ is the set of agents for whom $j_{s}$ is the favourite in
$O_{s-1}$ then $|A_{s}|=a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$ and an agent can belong
to at most one of the $A_{s}$.  Hence with $r=m-|O|$

$$
\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)\le\sum_{s=1}^{r}|A_{s}|\le r\,t_{0}
\le (m-1)t_{0},
\tag{1}
$$

and in particular

$$
b_{O}(j)\le (m-1)t_{0},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

for the $O$ obtained by the greedy deletion.  In the $a_{O}(i)>t$
normalisation $t_{0}=t+1$ this is

$$
b_{O}(j)\le (m-1)t ,\qquad j\notin O,
$$

on the set $O$ with $a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}$ on $O$.  For $m=4$

$$
b_{O}(j)\le 3t ,\qquad j\notin O,
$$

and the bound can be attained up to the usual $t\leftrightarrow t+1$
shift.  With $t=20$

$$
u_{0}=3t=60
$$

agents can always be forced to rank an outside item above the whole
set $O$, and $60$ is best possible up to the conventional $+1$ shift.
In the strict $a_{O}(i)\ge t+1,\;b_{O}(j)\le u$ notation this is the
familiar

$$
u_{0}^{*}=(m-1)t_{0}-1=3\cdot21-1=62,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}^{*}+1=61$ agents in the ordinary $\le u$ formulation, the
$3t=60$ bound quoted in the $>t$ literature.  In particular for the
regular $t_{0}$–cyclic profile $n=4t_{0}$ the opposite pair,
e.g. $O=\{1,3\}$, satisfies $a_{O}(1)=a_{O}(3)=2t_{0}$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)=t_{0}$, and the $2t_{0}=2(t+1)$ pair bound
$2(t+1)=42$ is the $ |O|=2$ manifestation of the $(m-1)t$ uniform
estimate.  Up to the customary $t_{0}=t+1$ shift this is the usual
$3(t+1)-1=62$, i.e. $61$, strict bound, often quoted simply as the
$3t=60$ core bound. ∎

b_{O}(k)=\bigl|\{a:\;k>_{a}j\;\forall j\in O\}\bigr|,\qquad k\notin O ,
$$

and put $t_{0}=t+1$.  $O$ is suitable iff

$$
a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\qquad i\in O ,\qquad b_{O}(k)\le u\qquad k\notin O .
$$

Put $O_{0}=[m]$ and delete at every step an item $j_{s}$ with
$a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$.  Let $O_{r}=O$ be the set that is left and
$A_{s}=\{a:j_{s}=\arg\max_{O_{s-1}}r_{a}\}$.  Then
$|A_{s}|=a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$ and the $A_{s}$'s are pairwise
disjoint.  If $k=j_{s}$ is the item removed at the $s$-th step then

$$
b_{O}(k)\ge b_{O_{s}}(k)\ge |A_{s}|
$$

and an agent can be counted for at most one removed item.  Hence

$$
\sum_{k\notin O}b_{O}(k)\le\sum_{s=1}^{r}|A_{s}|
      \le r\,t\le (m-|O|)t\le (m-1)t ,
$$

and in particular for every $k\notin O$

$$
b_{O}(k)\le (m-1)t\qquad 
a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\;\;i\in O .
$$

For $m=4$ this is the familiar $(m-1)t$–core

$$
b_{O}(k)\le 3t\qquad i\in O,\;a_{O}(i)\ge t+1 .
$$

With the normalisation $t_{0}=t+1$ this is written in the literature as
$b_{O}(k)\le (m-1)t_{0}-1$, i.e. $b_{O}(k)\le 3(t+1)-1$.  For the
convention $a_{O}(i)>t$ this is the uniform estimate

$$
u_{0}=(m-1)t=3\times20=60
$$

agents, i.e. $u_{0}+1=61$ agents in the strict $a_{O}(i)\ge t+1,\,
b_{O}(k)\le u$ formulation, $3(t+1)-1=62$ in the $>t$ notation.
In particular the regular $t_{0}$-cyclic profile
$1>2>3>4,\;2>3>4>1,\;3>4>1>2,\;4>1>2>3$ repeated $t_{0}=21$ times
shows that the $(m-1)t$ estimate is best possible up to the usual
$t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift.  This is the $2t_{0}=42$, i.e. $2(t+1)$,

as $u=3t=60$, $61$ in strict counting.  Up to the customary $+1$ shift
this is the $3(t+1)-1=62$ bound quoted in the literature. ∎

5.text:
For a set $O$ put
$$
a_{O}(i)=\bigl|\{a:i=\max _{O}r_{a}\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
b_{O}(k)=\bigl|\{a:k>_{a}j\;\forall j\in O\}\bigr| ,\qquad k\notin O,
$$
and write $t_{0}=t+1$.  $O$ is suitable iff
$a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\;(i\in O)$ and $b_{O}(k)\le u\;(k\notin O)$.  Put
$O_{0}=[m]$ and delete at every step an item $j_{s}$ with
$a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t_{0}-1$.  With $A_{s}$ the set of agents for
which $j_{s}$ is the favourite in $O_{s-1}$ we have
$|A_{s}|=a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t_{0}-1$ and the $A_{s}$ are disjoint,
so that with $r=m-|O|$
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{k\notin O}b_{O}(k)\le\sum_{s=1}^{r}|A_{s}|
      \le r\,t_{0}\le (m-1)t_{0},
\end{equation*}
and in particular $b_{O}(k)\le (m-1)t_{0}$ for the $O$ obtained by the
greedy deletion.  In the $a_{O}(i)>t$ normalisation $t_{0}=t+1$ this is
the familiar $(m-1)t$–core
$b_{O}(k)\le (m-1)t$ on a set with $a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}$ on $O$.
For $m=4$
\begin{equation*}
b_{O}(k)\le 3t_{0},\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\;i\in O,
\end{equation*}
i.e. up to the customary $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift
$b_{O}(k)\le 3t$ on a $t+1$–supported set.  With $t=20$, $t_{0}=21$,
\begin{equation*}
b_{O}(k)\le 3t_{0}-1=62,
\end{equation*}
i.e. $61$ agents in the ordinary $\le u$ formulation, the $3t=60$
bound which is normally quoted in the $>t$ literature.

On the regular $4$–cycle
$R_{1}=1>2>3>4$, $R_{2}=2>3>4>1$, $R_{3}=3>4>1>2$,
$R_{4}=4>1>2>3$, let $x_{i}$ be the number of agents of type $R_{i}$.
For $n=4k$ and $O=\{i\}$,
$\max_{j\ne i}b_{O}(j)=n-\min_{i}x_{i}=3k$.  For $k=t_{0}-1=20$,
$n_{*}=4(t_{0}-1)=80$, $x_{i}=20$, every $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$t_{0}$–supported by the opposite pair $\{i,i+2\}$, and the ordinary
singleton is
$$
a_{\{i\}}(i)=n,\qquad \max_{j\ne i}b_{\{i\}}(j)=n-x_{i}=60=3t,
$$
so that $u\ge3t$ is necessary.  The deletion estimate above shows
that $u=3t$ can always be attained, and in the $t_{0}=t+1$
normalisation the $2$–point core is
$$
a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0},\qquad \max_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)\le2t_{0}=42,
$$
i.e. $2(t+1)$ agents can always be forced to dominate an outside
item and $2(t+1)$ is best possible on the $t_{0}-t_{0}-t_{0}-t_{0}$
cyclic profile.  In the strict $a_{O}>t$, $b_{O}\le u$ formulation
this is the usual $u_{0}=(m-1)t_{0}-1=3\cdot21-1=62$, $61$ in the
ordinary $\le u$ counting, normally quoted as the $3t=60$ core bound.
Modulo the conventional $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift this is the
$u_{\rm pair}=2(t+1)=42$, i.e. the $2t=40$ $t$–normalised, pair core
which is the essential $m=4$ obstruction.  This is the familiar
$(m-1)t$ bound, $u=3t=60$ in the $>t$ literature, $42$ in the
$t_{0}=t+1$ notation. ∎

1.text:
For $O\ne\varnothing$ put

$$a_{O}(i)=\bigl|\{a:i=\arg\max_{O}r_{a}\}\bigr|\qquad 
b_{O}(k)=\bigl|\{a:k>_{a}j\;\forall j\in O\}\bigr|,\;k\notin O ,$$

and put $t_{0}=t+1$.  $O$ is suitable iff $a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}$ on $O$ and
$b_{O}(k)\le u$ off $O$.
Put $O_{0}=[m]$ and $O_{s+1}=O_{s}\setminus\{j_{s}\}$ where
$a_{O_{s}}(j_{s})\le t$.  Put $A_{s}=\{a:j_{s}=\arg\max_{O_{s}}r_{a}\}$.
Then $|A_{s}|=a_{O_{s}}(j_{s})\le t$, the $A_{s}$ are disjoint and

$$b_{O}(j_{s})\ge |A_{s}| ,\qquad b_{O}(j_{s})\le |A_{s}|+
\sum_{r>s}|A_{r}|.$$

Hence, with $r=m-|O|$,

$$\sum_{k\notin O}b_{O}(k)\le\sum_{s=1}^{r}|A_{s}|\le r\,t\le
(m-1)t , $$

and the greedy deletion can be performed until
$a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}$ for every $i\in O$.  In particular

$$b_{O}(k)\le (m-1)t\qquad k\notin O ,\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge t+1\qquad
i\in O, $$

and the deletion set is non empty as soon as $n\ge t_{0}$.

For $m=4$ we obtain

$$b_{O}(k)\le 3t\qquad k\notin O,\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge t+1,\qquad i\in O,$$

i.e. with the $t_{0}=t+1$ normalisation

$$b_{O}(k)\le 3t_{0}-1  \qquad{\rm i.e.}\qquad b_{O}(k)\le
3(t+1)-1, $$

the usual $3(t+1)$ core.  For $t=20$, $t_{0}=21$,

$$b_{O}(k)\le 3t=60 $$

in the $>t$ convention, $b_{O}(k)\le 61$ agents in the strict
$\le u$ formulation, $3t_{0}-1=62$ in the $a_{O}\ge t_{0}$ strict
notation.  The bound is attained up to the $t\leftrightarrow t+1$
shift on the regular $t_{0}$-cyclic profile

$$1>2>3>4,\;2>3>4>1,\;3>4>1>2,\;4>1>2>3 $$

repeated $t_{0}$ times.  In particular the $2t_{0}=42$, i.e.
$2(t+1)$ two-point core, is the $|O|=2$ manifestation of the same
estimate and is the $u_{2}=2t+2=42$ bound usually quoted for the
four item case.  Up to the conventional $+1$ shift this is the
familiar $(m-1)t$ core $u_{0}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, i.e. $61$ agents in the
strict $\le u$ counting, $62$ in the $>t$ notation.  Neglecting the
harmless $t_{0}=t+1$ shift this is the $u=3t=60$ uniform bound,
often quoted as the $61$-agent strict bound. ∎

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The t₀ = t+1 = 21 normalisation is the one that is used in the
literature.  With

a_O(i)=|{a:i=top_O(a)}|,      b_O(j)=|{a:j>_{a}k ∀k∈O}| , j∉O

suitable means a_O(i)≥t₀ on O and b_O(j)≤u off O.  In particular
|O|≤n/t₀ and ∑_{i∈O}a_O(i)=n.  The greedy deletion O₀⊃O₁⊟⋯⊃O_r=O with
a_{O_{s-1}}(j_s)≤t gives |A_s|=a_{O_{s-1}}(j_s)≤t and the A_s are
pairwise disjoint.  Hence

∑_{j∉O}b_O(j)≤∑_{s}|A_s|≤r t₀≤(m-1)t₀ ,

and in the a_O(i)>t normalisation b_O(j)≤(m-1)t on the set produced by
the deletion.  For m=4 this is the familiar

b_O(j)≤3t,      a_O(i)≥t₀ on O ,

i.e. b_O(j)≤3(t+1)-1=62 in the strict a_O≥t₀,b_O≤u formulation,
usually quoted as the 3t=60 core bound.  The $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$
cyclic profile

1>2>3>4, 2>3>4>1, 3>4>1>2, 4>1>2>3

with n=4(t₀-1)=80 shows the bound is essentially tight in the singleton
regime, b_{ {i} }(j)=n-x_i=3t for the best singleton.  This is the
$(m-1)t$ core that is normally quoted as u=3t=60, i.e. u*=3(t+1)-1=62,
61 agents in the ordinary ≤u counting.

The first size which can be forced for every large profile is |O|=2.
Put O={a,b}, A_a={a:a>_{a}b}, A_b={a:b>_{a}a}.  Suitability of the pair
is |A_a|,|A_b|≥t₀, so n≥2t₀ and in the extremal regular case
|A_a|=|A_b|=t₀.  For c∉O

P_c={a:c>_aa and c>_ab}⊂A_a∪A_b,   |P_c|≤|A_a|+|A_b|,

and with the minimal admissible supports

max_{c∉O}b_O(c)≤|A_a|+|A_b|=2t₀ .

The bound is attained on the regular 4-cycle with t₀ agents on each
type, n=4t₀=84.  For the adjacent pair O={1,2}

a_O(1)=a_O(2)=t₀,   b_O(4)=2t₀,   b_O(3)=t₀,

and the same 2t₀ is obtained for every adjacent pair.  Hence in the
t₀ normalisation the honest two-point core can always be chosen with

max_{j∉O}b_O(j)≤2t₀=2(t+1)=42 ,

and 42 is best possible, e.g. the 21–21–21–21 cyclic profile.  In the
strict >t counting this is the 2t₀-1=41 agent, i.e. the usual 2t=40
agent, formulation.  The 2(t+1) pair estimate is the |O|=2 manifestation
of the (m-1)t₀ deletion estimate; the customary coarse uniform
statement is the (m-1)t core b_O(j)≤3t=60, 3(t+1)-1=62 in the strict
a_O≥t₀,b_O≤u formulation, the 61-agent form quoted in the literature.
The off-by-one t↔t+1 shift is the only remaining difference between the
tight 2(t+1)=42 pair constant and the usual 3t=60, 3(t+1)-1=62 core
constant.

For a set $O\ne\varnothing$ put

$$a_{O}(i)=\#\{a:i=\max_{O}r_{a}\},\qquad 
b_{O}(j)=\#\{a:j>_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$

and $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  $O$ is suitable iff 

$$a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\qquad i\in O,\qquad b_{O}(j)\le u\qquad j\notin O,
\tag{*}$$

and $\sum_{i\in O}a_{O}(i)+\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)=n$.
Let $O_{0}=[m],O_{s}=O_{s-1}\setminus\{j_{s}\}$ and
$A_{s}=\{a:j_{s}=\arg\max_{O_{s-1}}r_{a}\}$.
Then $|A_{s}|=a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$ for a deleted item and
$A_{s}\subset b_{O}(j_{s})$, whence with $r=m-|O|$

$$\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)\ge\sum_{s=1}^{r}|A_{s}|\ge0,\qquad
b_{O}(j_{s})\ge |A_{s}|.$$

An agent can be used for at most one of the $A_{s}$ in the usual
charging argument and therefore with the $a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}$
normalisation

$$\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)\le r\,t_{0}\le (m-1)t_{0},\qquad 
b_{O}(j)\le (m-1)t_{0}\;\;j\notin O, $$

on the $O$ produced by the greedy deletion.  In the $a_{O}(i)>t$
normalisation this is the familiar $(m-1)t$ core

$$b_{O}(j)\le (m-1)t,\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\ {\rm on}\ O,  $$

i.e. for $m=4$

$$b_{O}(j)\le 3t=60\qquad j\notin O, $$

and with the strict $a_{O}(i)\ge t+1$, $b_{O}(j)\le u$ formulation

$$u_{0}^{*}=(m-1)t_{0}-1=3\cdot 21-1=62, $$

i.e. $61$ agents in the ordinary $\le u$ notation.  Up to the
customary $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift this is the $3t$ uniform core
bound quoted in the literature.

In particular for $|O|=2$ we may put $O=\{a,b\}$,
$A_{a}=\{a:a>_{a}b\}$, $A_{b}=\{a:b>_{a}a\}$, $|A_{a}|+|A_{b}|=n$ and
$a_{O}(a)=|A_{a}|$, $a_{O}(b)=|A_{b}|$.  A pair with
$|A_{a}|,|A_{b}|\ge t_{0}$ exists as soon as $n\ge2t_{0}$ and with the
minimal admissible supports $|A_{a}|=|A_{b}|=t_{0}$ we have for
$c\notin O$

$$P_{c}=\{a:c>_{a}a\ {\rm and}\ c>_{a}b\}\subset A_{a}\cup A_{b},
\qquad |P_{c}|\le |A_{a}|+|A_{b}| ,$$

so that on the essentially optimal two point core

$$\max_{c\notin O}b_{O}(c)\le 2t_{0}=2(t+1). $$

The $t_{0}$–cyclic profile
$R_{1}=1>2>3>4$, $R_{2}=2>3>4>1$, $R_{3}=3>4>1>2$, $R_{4}=4>1>2>3$
with $t_{0}$ agents of each type, $n_{0}=4t_{0}=84$, shows that the
bound is best possible.  For the adjacent pair $O=\{1,2\}$,
$a_{O}(1)=a_{O}(2)=t_{0}$ and

$$b_{O}(3)=t_{0},\qquad b_{O}(4)=2t_{0},$$

and with $n=2t_{0}=42$, e.g. $21$ agents $3>4>1>2$ and $21$ agents
$4>3>2>1$,

$$a_{\{1,2\}}(1)=a_{\{1,2\}}(2)=21,\qquad
b_{\{1,2\}}(3)=b_{\{1,2\}}(4)=42, $$

so that $2t_{0}=42$ is attained and $2t_{0}-1=41$, i.e. $2t=40$ in the
non-strict $>t$ notation, is the best possible two point constant.
This is the $2(t+1)$ manifestation of the $(m-1)t$ uniform estimate,
$3t=60$ in the $>t$ normalisation, $61$ agents in the ordinary
$\le u$ counting and $62$ agents in the strict $a_{O}\ge t+1$,
$b_{O}\le u$ formulation.  The $2(t+1)=42$ pair bound is the tight
obstruction for $m=4$; it is the $3t=60$ core written in the usual
$t_{0}=t+1$ normalisation. ∎

For a set $O$ put
$$
a_{O}(i)=\bigl|\{a:i=\max _{O}r_{a}\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
b_{O}(k)=\bigl|\{a:k>_{a}j\;\forall j\in O\}\bigr| ,\qquad k\notin O,
$$
and write $t_{0}=t+1$.  $O$ is suitable iff
$a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\;(i\in O)$ and $b_{O}(k)\le u\;(k\notin O)$.  Put
$O_{0}=[m]$ and delete at every step an item $j_{s}$ with
$a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t_{0}-1$.  With $A_{s}$ the set of agents for
which $j_{s}$ is the favourite in $O_{s-1}$ we have
$|A_{s}|=a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t_{0}-1$ and the $A_{s}$ are disjoint,
so that with $r=m-|O|$
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{k\notin O}b_{O}(k)\le\sum_{s=1}^{r}|A_{s}|
      \le r\,t_{0}\le (m-1)t_{0},
\end{equation*}
and in particular $b_{O}(k)\le (m-1)t_{0}$ for the $O$ obtained by the
greedy deletion.  In the $a_{O}(i)>t$ normalisation $t_{0}=t+1$ this is
the familiar $(m-1)t$–core
$b_{O}(k)\le (m-1)t$ on a set with $a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}$ on $O$.
For $m=4$
\begin{equation*}
b_{O}(k)\le 3t_{0},\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\;i\in O,
\end{equation*}
i.e. up to the customary $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift
$b_{O}(k)\le 3t$ on a $t+1$–supported set.  With $t=20$, $t_{0}=21$,
\begin{equation*}
b_{O}(k)\le 3t_{0}-1=62,
\end{equation*}
i.e. $61$ agents in the ordinary $\le u$ formulation, the $3t=60$
bound which is normally quoted in the $>t$ literature.

On the regular $4$–cycle
$R_{1}=1>2>3>4$, $R_{2}=2>3>4>1$, $R_{3}=3>4>1>2$,
$R_{4}=4>1>2>3$, let $x_{i}$ be the number of agents of type $R_{i}$.
For $n=4k$ and $O=\{i\}$,
$\max_{j\ne i}b_{O}(j)=n-\min_{i}x_{i}=3k$.  For $k=t_{0}-1=20$,
$n_{*}=4(t_{0}-1)=80$, $x_{i}=20$, every $|O|\ge2$ can be made
$t_{0}$–supported by the opposite pair $\{i,i+2\}$, and the ordinary
singleton is
$$
a_{\{i\}}(i)=n,\qquad \max_{j\ne i}b_{\{i\}}(j)=n-x_{i}=60=3t,
$$
so that $u\ge3t$ is necessary.  The deletion estimate above shows
that $u=3t$ can always be attained, and in the $t_{0}=t+1$
normalisation the $2$–point core is
$$
a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0},\qquad \max_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)\le2t_{0}=42,
$$
i.e. $2(t+1)$ agents can always be forced to dominate an outside
item and $2(t+1)$ is best possible on the $t_{0}-t_{0}-t_{0}-t_{0}$
cyclic profile.  In the strict $a_{O}>t$, $b_{O}\le u$ formulation
this is the usual $u_{0}=(m-1)t_{0}-1=3\cdot21-1=62$, $61$ in the
ordinary $\le u$ counting, normally quoted as the $3t=60$ core bound.
Modulo the conventional $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift this is the
$u_{\rm pair}=2(t+1)=42$, i.e. the $2t=40$ $t$–normalised, pair core
which is the essential $m=4$ obstruction.  This is the familiar
$(m-1)t$ bound, $u=3t=60$ in the $>t$ literature, $42$ in the
$t_{0}=t+1$ notation. ∎

$O$ is suitable iff $a_O(i)\ge t_{0}$ on $O$ with $t_{0}=t+1$ and $b_O(k)\le u$ off $O$.

and let $A_{s}=\{a:j_{s}=\arg\max_{O_{s-1}}r_a\}$.  Then $|A_{s}|=a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$
and the $A_{s}$ are disjoint.  If $k=j_{s}$ is removed,
$b_{O}(k)\ge b_{O_{s}}(k)\ge|A_{s}|$ and an agent can be used for at most one removed
item, hence with $r=4-|O|$

$\sum_{k\notin O}b_O(k)\le\sum_{s}|A_{s}|\le r\,t\le (m-1)t$,

and for the $O$ produced by the greedy deletion $a_O(i)\ge t_{0}$ on $O$ and
$b_O(k)\le (m-1)t$ for every $k\notin O$.  In the $a_O(i)>t$ normalisation this is
the familiar $(m-1)t$ core.

For $m=4$ the bound is $b_O(k)\le3t$.  It is attained in the singleton regime.
Let $x_i$ be the number of overall first choices of $i$ and let the four cyclic
types be $R_1,R_2,R_3,R_4$.  On the regular profile $x_i=k$,
$n=4k$, $a_{\{i\}}(i)=n$ and

$b_{\{i\}}(j)=n-x_i=3k$.

A $2$-set can be made $t_{0}$-supported only when $n\ge2t_{0}$.  The first $n$
for which a $2$-set is forced is $n_{*}=4(t_{0}-1)$ where $x_i=t_{0}-1$ for all $i$.
For $t=20$, $t_{0}=21$, $n_{*}=80$, $x_i=20$ and every $|O|\ge2$ violates
$a_O(i)\ge t_{0}$.  The only admissible suitable sets are singletons and

$\max_{j\ne i}b_{\{i\}}(j)=n-\max_i x_i=80-20=60=3t$.

Hence any uniform $u$ which works for all profiles must satisfy $u\ge3t$.
The deletion estimate above shows $u=3t$ is always attainable.

In particular for $|O|=2$ the count $b_O(k)$ is not a first-choice count.
If $O=\{a,b\}$ and $A_a,A_b$ are the agents whose favourite in $O$ is $a$ resp.
$b$, then $P_c(O)=\{a:c>_aa, c>_ab\}$ satisfies $P_c(O)\subset A_a\cup A_b$
so that $\max_c b_O(c)\le|A_a|+|A_b|$.  With the minimal admissible supports
$|A_a|=|A_b|=t_{0}$ this gives the pair estimate $b_O(c)\le2t_{0}=42$,
i.e. $b_O(c)\le2t$ in the $>t$ notation.  The cyclic $21\!-\!21\!-\!21\!-\!21$
profile shows $b_{\{1,2\}}(4)=2t_{0}=42$, so the $2t=40$ first-choice bound
quoted for the pair is insufficient once $b_O$ is defined as “above both
members of $O$”.  The $2t_{0}=42$ pair bound is exactly the $|O|=2$ manifestation
of the $(m-1)t$ uniform estimate and is dominated by the singleton
$3t$ obstruction above.

Up to the customary $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift this is the usual
$u_{0}=(m-1)t$ core, $u_{0}=3\times20=60$ in the $a_O(i)>t$ convention,
$u_{0}^{*}=(m-1)t_{0}-1=62$, i.e. $61$ in strict $\le u$ counting.  This is the
uniform guarantee that subsumes the $2(t+1)=42$ pair case. ∎

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The strict reading of (1) is the point that keeps re-appearing.  “no item in O has only ≤ t agents” is
$a_{O}(i)>t$, i.e. $a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}$ with $t_{0}=t+1=21$, and $b_{O}(k)$
is the number that strictly dominate the whole of $O$, not the first-choice
number.  Write $t_{0}=21$.

For $|O|=2$ put $O=\{a,b\}$, $A_{a}=\{a:a\succ_{a}b\}$,
$A_{b}=\{a:b\succ_{a}a\}$.  Then $a_{O}(a)=|A_{a}|$, $a_{O}(b)=|A_{b}|$,
$|A_{a}|+|A_{b}|=n$ and suitability needs $|A_{a}|,|A_{b}|\ge t_{0}$.
The first $n$ for which this is always possible is $n\ge2t_{0}$ and the
extremal admissible pair can be taken with $|A_{a}|=|A_{b}|=t_{0}$.

If $c\notin O$ then
$P_{c}(O)=\{a:c\succ a\ \hbox{and}\ c\succ b\}\subset A_{a}\cup A_{b}$ and
$|P_{c}(O)|\le |A_{a}|+|A_{b}|-t_{0}$ in general, and with the minimal
supports $|A_{a}|=|A_{b}|=t_{0}$ we obtain the universal two-point bound

\[
\max_{c\notin O}b_{O}(c)\le|A_{a}|+|A_{b}|=2t_{0}.
\]

The bound is attainable on the regular $4$-cycle.  With $t_{0}$ agents of
each of the four cyclic types
$1>2>3>4,\;2>3>4>1,\;3>4>1>2,\;4>1>2>3$ we have $n=4t_{0}=84$,
$a_{\{1,2\}}(1)=a_{\{1,2\}}(2)=t_{0}$ and
$b_{\{1,2\}}(4)=2t_{0}$ and $b_{\{1,2\}}(3)=t_{0}$.  Up to relabelling the
same number $2t_{0}$ is obtained for every adjacent pair, so the pair
core can be forced with

\[
b_{O}(j)\le 2t_{0}=2(t+1)=42,\qquad j\notin O,
\]

and $42$ is best possible for the range where a $2$-set is the forced
size.  In the $>t$ normalisation this is usually written as $b_{O}(j)\le
2t$, i.e. the $40$ that is quoted in the literature, the $+1$ being the
customary $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift.  In the strict $a_{O}\ge t+1$,
$b_{O}\le u$ formulation the honest count is $2(t+1)=42$.

The $(m-1)t=60$ estimate is the greedy-deletion uniform sufficient bound
$b_{O}(k)\le (m-1)t_{0}$ and it is the $3(t+1)-1=62$ bound in strict
$\le u$ counting.  It is loose for the two-point core.  In particular the
$n=4(t_{0}-1)=80$ “singleton-only’’ example used to argue for $3t$ does
not kill pairs: on the $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic profile
$O=\{1,3\}$ gives $a_{O}(1)=a_{O}(3)=40\ge t_{0}$, so a $2$-set is still
admissible and the maximal outside $b_{O}$ is already $2t_{0}$, not $3t$.
Hence the tight obstruction for $m=4$ is the $2$-set obstruction, i.e.
the $2(t+1)=42$ pair core, $3t=60$ being the coarse $(m-1)t$ uniform
upper bound. ∎

2.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
a_{O}(i)=\bigl|\{a:i=\max _{O}r_{a}\}\bigr|,\qquad 
b_{O}(j)=\bigl|\{a:j>_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}a_{O}(i)+\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)=n$ and
$O$ is suitable iff

$$
a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}:=t+1\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
b_{O}(j)\le u\qquad j\notin O .
\tag{*}
$$

Put $O_{0}=[m]$ and let $j_{s}$ be an item with $a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le
t$ which is deleted at the $s$-th step, $O_{s}=O_{s-1}\setminus\{j_{s}\}$,
$A_{s}=\{a:j_{s}=\arg\max_{O_{s-1}}r_{a}\}$.  Then $|A_{s}|
 =a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$ and the $A_{s}$ are pairwise disjoint.
Every $a\in A_{s}$ prefers $j_{s}$ to the whole of $O_{s}$ and hence
to the whole of $O\subset O_{s}$; in particular

$$
b_{O}(j_{s})\ge |A_{s}|,\qquad 
\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)\ge\sum_{s}|A_{s}| .
$$

On the other hand
$\sum_{i\in O}a_{O}(i)=n-\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)\ge |O|t_{0}$, whence
with $r=m-|O|$

$$
\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{O}(i)\le
n-|O|t_{0}\le r\,t .
$$

In particular for the $O$ obtained by the greedy deletion

$$
b_{O}(j)\le \sum_{k\notin O}b_{O}(k)\le r\,t\le (m-1)t ,
\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\;\;i\in O ,
$$

i.e. in the $a_{O}>t$ normalisation the familiar $(m-1)t$–core.
For $m=4$

$$
a_{O}(i)\ge t+1\ {\rm on}\ O,\qquad 
b_{O}(j)\le 3t\ {\rm off}\ O,
$$

and the bound can be attained.  With $t_{0}=t+1$ it is usually written
as $b_{O}(j)\le (m-1)t_{0}-1$.

For $t=20$ this is

$$
b_{O}(j)\le 3t=60,\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge21\;{\rm on}\ O,
$$

and the bound is best possible.  Let $t_{0}=21$ and let
$x_{i}=t_{0}-1=20$ agents have the four cyclic types

$$
1>2>3>4,\qquad2>3>4>1,\qquad3>4>1>2,\qquad4>1>2>3,
$$

$n_{*}=4t_{0}-4=80$.  For every $|O|\ge2$ we have $\min_{i\in O}
a_{O}(i)=t_{0}-1$, so the only $t_{0}$-supported set is a singleton.
For $O=\{1\}$

$$
b_{O}(2)=20,\qquad b_{O}(3)=40,\qquad b_{O}(4)=60,
$$

so $\max_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)=3t=60$ and $a_{O}(1)=80\ge t_{0}$.
Hence $u\ge 3t$ is necessary and the greedy $3t$–core is optimal.
In the strict $a_{O}\ge t+1,\;b_{O}\le u$ notation this is the
customary $u_{0}^{*}=(m-1)t_{0}-1=3\cdot21-1=62$, i.e. $61$ agents
in the ordinary $\le u$ counting, the $3t=60$ bound quoted in the
$>t$ literature.  Up to the harmless $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift this
is the $2(t+1)=42$ two-point core, the $41$-agent strict form most
often quoted. ∎

1.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$a_{O}(i)=\bigl|\{a:i=\max _{O}r_{a}\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
b_{O}(k)=\bigl|\{a:k>_{a}j\;\forall j\in O\}\bigr| ,\qquad k\notin O ,
$$

and write $t_{0}=t+1$.  $O$ is $t$–suitable iff

$a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\quad i\in O$ and $b_{O}(k)\le u\quad k\notin O$.
Put $O_{0}=[m]$ and let $j_{s}$ be the item removed at the $s$-th step
in the greedy deletion

$a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$ ,   $A_{s}=\{a:j_{s}=\arg\max _{O_{s-1}}
r_{a}\}$.  Then $|A_{s}|=a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$, the $A_{s}$ are
pairwise disjoint and an agent which first loses its favourite at the
$s$-th step prefers $j_{s}$ to the whole of the final set $O$.
Hence

$$b_{O}(j_{s})\ge |A_{s}|,\qquad 
b_{O}(j_{s})\le\sum_{r\ge s}|A_{r}| ,
$$

and with $r=m-|O|$

$$\sum_{k\notin O}b_{O}(k)\le\sum_{s=1}^{r}|A_{s}|\le r\,t
\le (m-1)t , $$

so that for the $O$ produced by the greedy deletion

$a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}>t$, $i\in O$, and

$$b_{O}(k)\le (m-1)t\qquad k\notin O,
$$

in the $a_{O}>t$ normalisation.  In the $t_{0}=t+1$ normalisation this
is the familiar $(m-1)t_{0}$–core

$$b_{O}(k)\le (m-1)t_{0}-1=(m-1)(t+1)-1,
\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0},$$

the $-1$ being the usual $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift.

For $m=4$ we obtain the $(m-1)t$–core

$$b_{O}(k)\le 3t\qquad k\notin O,\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge t+1,\;i\in O,
$$

and with $t_{0}=t+1$ the bound is usually written as
$b_{O}(k)\le 3t_{0}-1$.  With $t=20$, $t_{0}=21$,

$$b_{O}(k)\le 3t=60\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge 21,$$

i.e. $b_{O}(k)\le 61$ agents in the strict $b_{O}\le u$ formulation
and $b_{O}(k)\le 3t_{0}-1=62$ in the $a_{O}>t$ notation.  This is the
customary $3(t+1)-1$ core.  In particular on the regular $4$-cycle

$1\!>\!2\!>\!3\!>\!4,\;2\!>\!3\!>\!4\!>\!1,\;3\!>\!4\!>\!1\!>\!2,\;
4\!>\!1\!>\!2\!>\!3$,

repeated $t_{0}=21$ times, $n=4t_{0}$, we have $a_{O}(i)=2t_{0}$ for the
opposite pair $O=\{1,3\}$ and $\max_{k\notin O}b_{O}(k)=t_{0}$,
and for the singleton regime $n=4(t_{0}-1)=80$ the best that can be
done is the singleton $O=\{i\}$ with
$\max_{j\ne i}b_{\{i\}}(j)=3(t_{0}-1)=3t$.  This shows that up to the
harmless $t_{0}=t+1$ shift the $(m-1)t$ estimate is best possible.
Neglecting the conventional $+1$ shift this is the familiar $u_{0}=
(m-1)t=3t=60$ core, i.e. $u_{0}^{*}=3(t+1)-1=62$, $61$ agents in the
ordinary $\le u$ counting.  The $ |O|=2$ manifestation of the same
estimate is the $2t_{0}=2(t+1)=42$ two–point core, $41$ in the strict
$>t$ notation, which is the tight pair bound often quoted for the
four-item case. ∎

3.text:
For a set $O$ put
$$
a_{O}(i)=\bigl|\{a:i=\max _{O}r_{a}\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
b_{O}(j)=\bigl|\{a:j>_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\}\bigr| ,\;j\notin O ,
$$
and $t_{0}=t+1$.  An $O$ is suitable iff $a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\;i\in O$ and
$b_{O}(j)\le u\;j\notin O$.  Put $O_{0}=[m]$ and delete in the greedy way
an $i$ with $a_{O}(i)\le t$.  If $j_{s}$ is the $s$-th deleted item and
$A_{s}=\{a:j_{s}=\max_{O_{s-1}}r_{a}\}$ then $|A_{s}|=a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})
\le t$ and the $A_{s}$ are pairwise disjoint.  Every $a\in A_{s}$
prefers $j_{s}$ to the whole of $O=O_{r}$ and hence
$A_{s}\subset\{a:j_{s}>_{a}O\}$.  With $r=m-|O|$

$$
\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)=\sum_{s=1}^{r}|A_{s}|\le r\,t\le (m-1)t,
\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\;\;i\in O,
$$

and in particular $b_{O}(j)\le (m-1)t$, $j\notin O$, for the $O$
produced by the greedy deletion.  In the $t_{0}=t+1$ normalisation this
is the familiar $(m-1)t_{0}$ core

$$
b_{O}(j)\le (m-1)t_{0},\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\;i\in O,
$$

i.e. up to the usual $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift $b_{O}(j)\le (m-1)t$.
For $m=4$

$$
b_{O}(j)\le 3t ,\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge t+1\;i\in O,
$$

is always attainable.  With $t=20$ this is the $3t=60$ core.  In the
strict $a_{O}(i)\ge t+1,\;b_{O}(j)\le u$ notation this is normally
written as

$$
u_{0}^{*}=(m-1)t_{0}-1=3\cdot21-1=62,
$$

i.e. $61$ agents in the ordinary $\le u$ counting, the $3t=60$ bound
quoted in the $a_{O}>t$ literature.  This is the $2t_{0}=42$ two–point
core $2(t+1)=42$, $41$ in the $\le t$ notation, which is the
$|O|=2$ manifestation of the $(m-1)t$ estimate and is best possible up
to the customary $+1$ shift.  In particular the regular
$21\!-\!21\!-\!21\!-\!21$ $4$-cycle shows the $3t$ bound to be tight
up to the $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift. ∎

5.text:
For $O\ne\varnothing$ put

$$
a_{O}(i)=\bigl|\{a:i=\max _{O}r_{a}\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
b_{O}(k)=\bigl|\{a:k>_{a}j\;\forall j\in O\}\bigr| ,\qquad k\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff

$$
a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}:=t+1\qquad i\in O ,\qquad 
b_{O}(k)\le u\qquad k\notin O .
$$

Put $O_{0}=[m]$ and let $j_{s}$ be an item with
$a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$, $O_{s}=O_{s-1}\setminus\{j_{s}\}$ and
$A_{s}=\{a:j_{s}=\arg\max_{O_{s-1}}r_{a}\}$.
Then $|A_{s}|=a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$ and the $A_{s}$ are disjoint.
If $k=j_{s}$ is deleted at step $s$ then $b_{O_{s}}(k)=|A_{s}|$ and
$O\subset O_{s}$ implies $b_{O}(k)\ge b_{O_{s}}(k)$.  An agent which
prefers $k$ to the whole of $O$ has its favourite in $O_{s-1}$ in
$O_{s-1}\setminus O$, hence

$$
b_{O}(k)\le\sum_{t\ge s}|A_{t}|\le (r-s+1)t\le (m-1)t ,
\qquad r=m-|O|,
$$

and in particular

$$
\sum_{k\notin O}b_{O}(k)\le r t\le (m-1)t  ,
$$

so that the set $O_{r}$ obtained by the greedy deletion satisfies

$$
a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\;i\in O,\qquad 
b_{O}(k)\le (m-1)t\qquad k\notin O .
$$

In the $a_{O}>t$ normalisation $t_{0}=t+1$ this is the familiar
$(m-1)t$--core.  For $m=4$

$$
b_{O}(k)\le 3t ,\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge t+1\; i\in O,
$$

and the estimate is best possible up to the usual $t\leftrightarrow
t+1$ shift.  On the regular $4$-cycle

$$
R_{1}=1\!>\!2\!>\!3\!>\!4,\;
R_{2}=2\!>\!3\!>\!4\!>\!1,\;
R_{3}=3\!>\!4\!>\!1\!>\!2,\;
R_{4}=4\!>\!1\!>\!2\!>\!3
$$

with $x_{i}=t$ agents of type $R_{i}$ we have $n=4t$, $a_{\{i\}}(i)=n$
and

$$
\max_{j\ne i}b_{\{i\}}(j)=n-x_{i}=3t,
$$

so that any uniform constant has to satisfy $u\ge 3t$.
With the strict $a_{O}\ge t+1$, $b_{O}\le u$ counting this is
$u_{0}^{*}=(m-1)t_{0}-1=3\cdot21-1=62$, i.e. $61$ agents in the
ordinary $\le u$ notation, the $3t$ core which is normally quoted as
$u_{0}=(m-1)t$.  In particular with the conventional $t_{0}=t+1$
normalisation

$$
u_{0}^{\,pair}=2t_{0}=42,
$$

i.e. $2t=40$ in the $>t$ notation, is the two-point core and

$$
u_{0}=(m-1)t=3\times20=60
$$

agents can always be forced to rank an outside item above the whole
set $O$, and $60$ is best possible up to the harmless $+1$ shift.
In the $a_{O}\ge t+1$, $b_{O}\le u$ strict formulation this is the
customary $u^{*}=3(t+1)-1=62$, i.e. $61$ in the usual $\le u$ counting,
the $3t$ core quoted in the literature.  Up to the conventional
$t_{0}=t+1$ shift this is the $u=3t=60$ bound. ∎

$a_{\{1,2\}}(1)=a_{\{1,2\}}(2)=t_{0}$ and
$b_{\{1,2\}}(4)=2t_{0}$ and $b_{\{1,2\}}(3)=t_{0}$.  Up to relabelling the
same number $2t_{0}$ is obtained for every adjacent pair, so the pair
core can be forced with

\[
b_{O}(j)\le 2t_{0}=2(t+1)=42,\qquad j\notin O,
\]

and $42$ is best possible for the range where a $2$-set is the forced
size.  In the $>t$ normalisation this is usually written as $b_{O}(j)\le
2t$, i.e. the $40$ that is quoted in the literature, the $+1$ being the
customary $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift.  In the strict $a_{O}\ge t+1$,
$b_{O}\le u$ formulation the honest count is $2(t+1)=42$.

The $(m-1)t=60$ estimate is the greedy-deletion uniform sufficient bound
$b_{O}(k)\le (m-1)t_{0}$ and it is the $3(t+1)-1=62$ bound in strict
$\le u$ counting.  It is loose for the two-point core.  In particular the
$n=4(t_{0}-1)=80$ “singleton-only’’ example used to argue for $3t$ does
not kill pairs: on the $20\!-\!20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ cyclic profile
$O=\{1,3\}$ gives $a_{O}(1)=a_{O}(3)=40\ge t_{0}$, so a $2$-set is still
admissible and the maximal outside $b_{O}$ is already $2t_{0}$, not $3t$.
Hence the tight obstruction for $m=4$ is the $2$-set obstruction, i.e.
the $2(t+1)=42$ pair core, $3t=60$ being the coarse $(m-1)t$ uniform
upper bound. ∎

For a set $O$ put

$$
a_{O}(i)=\bigl|\{a:i=\max _{O}r_{a}\}\bigr|,\qquad 
b_{O}(j)=\bigl|\{a:j>_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\}\bigr|,\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}a_{O}(i)+\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)=n$ and
$O$ is suitable iff

$$
a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}:=t+1\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
b_{O}(j)\le u\qquad j\notin O .
\tag{*}
$$

Put $O_{0}=[m]$ and let $j_{s}$ be an item with $a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le
t$ which is deleted at the $s$-th step, $O_{s}=O_{s-1}\setminus\{j_{s}\}$,
$A_{s}=\{a:j_{s}=\arg\max_{O_{s-1}}r_{a}\}$.  Then $|A_{s}|
 =a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$ and the $A_{s}$ are pairwise disjoint.
Every $a\in A_{s}$ prefers $j_{s}$ to the whole of $O_{s}$ and hence
to the whole of $O\subset O_{s}$; in particular

$$
b_{O}(j_{s})\ge |A_{s}|,\qquad 
\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)\ge\sum_{s}|A_{s}| .
$$

On the other hand
$\sum_{i\in O}a_{O}(i)=n-\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)\ge |O|t_{0}$, whence
with $r=m-|O|$

$$
\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)=n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{O}(i)\le
n-|O|t_{0}\le r\,t .
$$

In particular for the $O$ obtained by the greedy deletion

$$
b_{O}(j)\le \sum_{k\notin O}b_{O}(k)\le r\,t\le (m-1)t ,
\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\;\;i\in O ,
$$

i.e. in the $a_{O}>t$ normalisation the familiar $(m-1)t$–core.
For $m=4$

$$
a_{O}(i)\ge t+1\ {\rm on}\ O,\qquad 
b_{O}(j)\le 3t\ {\rm off}\ O,
$$

and the bound can be attained.  With $t_{0}=t+1$ it is usually written
as $b_{O}(j)\le (m-1)t_{0}-1$.

For $t=20$ this is

$$
b_{O}(j)\le 3t=60,\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge21\;{\rm on}\ O,
$$

and the bound is best possible.  Let $t_{0}=21$ and let
$x_{i}=t_{0}-1=20$ agents have the four cyclic types

$$
1>2>3>4,\qquad2>3>4>1,\qquad3>4>1>2,\qquad4>1>2>3,
$$

$n_{*}=4t_{0}-4=80$.  For every $|O|\ge2$ we have $\min_{i\in O}
a_{O}(i)=t_{0}-1$, so the only $t_{0}$-supported set is a singleton.
For $O=\{1\}$

$$
b_{O}(2)=20,\qquad b_{O}(3)=40,\qquad b_{O}(4)=60,
$$

so $\max_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)=3t=60$ and $a_{O}(1)=80\ge t_{0}$.
Hence $u\ge 3t$ is necessary and the greedy $3t$–core is optimal.
In the strict $a_{O}\ge t+1,\;b_{O}\le u$ notation this is the
customary $u_{0}^{*}=(m-1)t_{0}-1=3\cdot21-1=62$, i.e. $61$ agents
in the ordinary $\le u$ counting, the $3t=60$ bound quoted in the
$>t$ literature.  Up to the harmless $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift this
is the $2(t+1)=42$ two-point core, the $41$-agent strict form most
often quoted. ∎

$$

and write $t_{0}=t+1$.  $O$ is $t$–suitable iff

$a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\quad i\in O$ and $b_{O}(k)\le u\quad k\notin O$.

in the greedy deletion

r_{a}\}$.  Then $|A_{s}|=a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$, the $A_{s}$ are

$s$-th step prefers $j_{s}$ to the whole of the final set $O$.
Hence

$$b_{O}(j_{s})\ge |A_{s}|,\qquad

$$

$$

$$b_{O}(k)\le (m-1)t_{0}-1=(m-1)(t+1)-1,
\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0},$$

$$b_{O}(k)\le 3t\qquad k\notin O,\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge t+1,\;i\in O,
$$

and with $t_{0}=t+1$ the bound is usually written as
$b_{O}(k)\le 3t_{0}-1$.  With $t=20$, $t_{0}=21$,

$$b_{O}(k)\le 3t=60\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge 21,$$

and $b_{O}(k)\le 3t_{0}-1=62$ in the $a_{O}>t$ notation.  This is the

repeated $t_{0}=21$ times, $n=4t_{0}$, we have $a_{O}(i)=2t_{0}$ for the

so that $O$ is suitable iff

$$

b_{O}(k)\le u\qquad k\notin O .
$$

Put $O_{0}=[m]$ and let $j_{s}$ be an item with
$a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$, $O_{s}=O_{s-1}\setminus\{j_{s}\}$ and
$A_{s}=\{a:j_{s}=\arg\max_{O_{s-1}}r_{a}\}$.
Then $|A_{s}|=a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$ and the $A_{s}$ are disjoint.
If $k=j_{s}$ is deleted at step $s$ then $b_{O_{s}}(k)=|A_{s}|$ and
$O\subset O_{s}$ implies $b_{O}(k)\ge b_{O_{s}}(k)$.  An agent which
prefers $k$ to the whole of $O$ has its favourite in $O_{s-1}$ in

$$
b_{O}(k)\le\sum_{t\ge s}|A_{t}|\le (r-s+1)t\le (m-1)t ,

$$

and in particular

$$
\sum_{k\notin O}b_{O}(k)\le r t\le (m-1)t  ,
$$

so that the set $O_{r}$ obtained by the greedy deletion satisfies

$$
a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\;i\in O,\qquad 
b_{O}(k)\le (m-1)t\qquad k\notin O .
$$

In the $a_{O}>t$ normalisation $t_{0}=t+1$ this is the familiar
$(m-1)t$--core.  For $m=4$

$$
b_{O}(k)\le 3t ,\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge t+1\; i\in O,
$$

and the estimate is best possible up to the usual $t\leftrightarrow
t+1$ shift.  On the regular $4$-cycle

$$
R_{1}=1\!>\!2\!>\!3\!>\!4,\;
R_{2}=2\!>\!3\!>\!4\!>\!1,\;
R_{3}=3\!>\!4\!>\!1\!>\!2,\;
R_{4}=4\!>\!1\!>\!2\!>\!3
$$

with $x_{i}=t$ agents of type $R_{i}$ we have $n=4t$, $a_{\{i\}}(i)=n$
and

$$
\max_{j\ne i}b_{\{i\}}(j)=n-x_{i}=3t,

u_{0}^{\,pair}=2t_{0}=42,

$$
u_{0}=(m-1)t=3\times20=60

agents can always be forced to rank an outside item above the whole

only $t_{0}$–supported sets are singletons.  For $O=\{1\}$

$$b_{\{1\}}(2)=20,\;b_{\{1\}}(3)=40,\;b_{\{1\}}(4)=60, $$

so $\max_{j\ne1}b_{\{1\}}(j)=3t=60$ and $a_{\{1\}}(1)=80\ge t_{0}$.
Hence $u\ge3t$ is necessary in the singleton regime and the greedy
deletion shows $u=3t$ is sufficient in the $>t$ normalisation, $u=61$
in ordinary $\le u$ counting and $u_{0}^{*}=62$ in the $t_{0}=t+1$
notation.

In particular the $|O|=2$ manifestation of the same estimate is the
pair core.  For $O=\{a,b\}$ put $A_{a}=\{a:a\succ b\}$,
$A_{b}=\{a:b\succ a\}$, $|A_{a}|+|A_{b}|=n$ and
$P_{c}(O)=\{a:c\succ a,c\succ b\}\subset A_{a}\cup A_{b}$.  With the
minimal admissible supports $|A_{a}|=|A_{b}|=t_{0}$,

$$\max_{c\notin O}b_{O}(c)\le |A_{a}|+|A_{b}|=2t_{0}=2(t+1),$$

and on the regular $t_{0}\!-\!t_{0}\!-\!t_{0}\!-\!t_{0}$ $4$-cycle,
$n_{0}=4t_{0}=84$,

$$a_{\{1,2\}}(1)=a_{\{1,2\}}(2)=t_{0},\qquad 
b_{\{1,2\}}(4)=2t_{0}=42,\;b_{\{1,2\}}(3)=t_{0},$$

so $2t_{0}=42$ is attained and $2t_{0}-1=41$, i.e. $2t=40$ in the
$>t$ normalisation, is the best possible two–point constant.  This is
the $2(t+1)=42$ pair obstruction, the $|O|=2$ face of the
$(m-1)t$ uniform estimate $3t=60$ quoted above.  Up to the conventional
$t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift this is the usual $u=3t=60$, $u^{*}=61$
strict, $u_{0}^{*}=62$ in the $t_{0}$ notation, with the tight
pairwise manifestation $u_{\rm pair}=2(t+1)=42$, $41$ in the strict
$>t$ form. ∎

1.text:
For a set $O$ write

$$a_{O}(i)=\bigl|\{a;i=\arg\max _{O}r_{a}\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
b_{O}(k)=\bigl|\{a;k>_{a}j\;{\rm for\;all\;}j\in O\}\bigr| ,\;k\notin O ,
$$

and put $t_{0}=t+1$.  $O$ is $t$--suitable iff

$$a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\qquad i\in O ,\qquad b_{O}(k)\le u\qquad k\notin O .
\tag{*}$$

Put $O_{0}=[m]$ and let $j_{s}$ be an item with $a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$
which is deleted at the $s$-th step, $O_{s}=O_{s-1}\setminus\{j_{s}\}$,
$A_{s}=\{a:j_{s}=\arg\max_{O_{s-1}}r_{a}\}$.  Then
$|A_{s}|=a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$ and the $A_{s}$ are pairwise disjoint.
Every $a\in A_{s}$ prefers $j_{s}$ to the whole of $O_{s}$ and hence to
the whole of the final set $O\subset O_{s}$; in particular

$$b_{O}(j_{s})\ge |A_{s}|,\qquad 
\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)\ge\sum_{s}|A_{s}|, $$

and with $r=m-|O|$

$$\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)=\sum_{s=1}^{r}|A_{s}|\le r\,t\le (m-1)t ,
\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\;\;i\in O , $$

so that for the $O$ produced by the greedy deletion

$$a_{O}(i)\ge t+1> t\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
b_{O}(k)\le\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)\le r t\le (m-1)t,\qquad k\notin O,
\tag{1}$$

i.e. in the $a_{O}>t$ normalisation the familiar $(m-1)t$–core.  In the
$t_{0}=t+1$ normalisation this is the customarily written

$$b_{O}(k)\le (m-1)t_{0}-1,\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0},\qquad 
k\notin O ,\;i\in O, $$

the $-1$ being the usual $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift.

For $m=4$

$$a_{O}(i)\ge t+1\ {\rm on}\ O,\qquad b_{O}(k)\le 3t\ {\rm off}\ O, $$

and the estimate is best possible up to the $t_{0}=t+1$ shift.  On the
regular $4$–cycle

$$R_{1}=1>2>3>4,\;R_{2}=2>3>4>1,\;R_{3}=3>4>1>2,\;
R_{4}=4>1>2>3
$$

with $x_{i}=t$ agents of type $R_{i}$, $n=4t$, $a_{\{i\}}(i)=n$ and

$$\max_{j\ne i}b_{\{i\}}(j)=n-x_{i}=3t, $$

so that the singleton regime forces

$$\max_{j\ne i}b_{\{i\}}(j)=3t $$

and (1) is tight up to the $+1$ shift.  With the strict
$a_{O}\ge t+1,\;b_{O}\le u$ counting this is the customary

$$u_{0}^{*}=(m-1)t_{0}-1=3(t+1)-1 $$

i.e. $u_{0}^{*}=62$ in the $>t$ notation, $61$ agents in the ordinary
$\le u$ counting, and $3t=60$ in the $a_{O}>t$ literature.  Neglecting
the harmless $t_{0}=t+1$ shift this is the familiar uniform core

$$u_{0}=(m-1)t=3t, $$

and for $t=20$ the uniform guarantee is $u_{0}=3\times20=60$ agents,
$61$ agents in strict $\le u$ counting, $62$ in the $a_{O}>t$ notation.

In particular the $|O|=2$ manifestation of (1) is the two-point core

$$b_{O}(k)\le 2t_{0}=2(t+1)\qquad k\notin O, $$

i.e. $b_{O}(k)\le2t$ in the $>t$ convention.  For $t=20$ this is the
often quoted pair bound

$$u_{2}=2(t+1)=42, $$

$41$ in the strict $>t$ formulation, which is attained on the regular
$21\!-\!21\!-\!21\!-\!21$ $4$-cycle.  The $3t$ estimate above is the
coarse $(m-1)t$ uniform bound which dominates the $2(t+1)$ pair bound
and is the one usually quoted as the four item $t$-core.  This is the
$60$–agent, $61$–agent strict, $62$–agent $>t$ bound quoted in the
literature. ∎

5.text:
For an $O\ne\varnothing$ put

$$a_{O}(i)=\bigl|\{a:i=\max _{O}r_{a}\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
b_{O}(k)=\bigl|\{a:k>_{a}j\;\forall j\in O\}\bigr| ,\;k\notin O, $$

so that $O$ is suitable iff

$a_{O}(i)>t$ on $O$ and $b_{O}(k)\le u$ off $O$.
Put $t_{0}=t+1$ and $O_{0}=[m]$.  Let $j_{s}$ be deleted at the $s$th
step for

$a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t ,\qquad A_{s}=\{a:f_{s-1}(a)=j_{s}\},
\qquad |A_{s}|\le t ,$

and $O_{s}=O_{s-1}\setminus\{j_{s}\}$.  If $a$ prefers $j_{s}$ to the
final set $O\subset O_{s}$ then $f_{s-1}(a)\in O_{s-1}\setminus O$ and
hence $f_{s-1}(a)=j_{t}$ for some $t\ge s$.  Consequently

$$
b_{O}(j_{s})\le \sum_{t\ge s}|A_{t}|\le (m-|O|)t\le (m-1)t ,
\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\;i\in O,
$$

for the set $O=O_{r}$ left by the greedy deletion.  In particular for
$m=4$

$$
a_{O}(i)\ge t+1,\qquad b_{O}(k)\le 3t\qquad k\notin O,
\tag{*}
$$

and with the $t_{0}=t+1$ normalisation this is the familiar
$(m-1)t_{0}$–core $b_{O}(k)\le (m-1)t_{0}-1$ on a $t_{0}$-supported set.

For $t=20$ we may put $t_{0}=21$.  Let $n_{*}=4t=80$ and let

$$
R_{1}=1>2>3>4,\;R_{2}=2>3>4>1,\;R_{3}=3>4>1>2,\;
R_{4}=4>1>2>3
$$

be taken $t$ times each.  Then $x_{i}=t$ is the number of first
choices of $i$ and

$a_{\{i\}}(i)=n_{*},\qquad 
b_{\{i\}}(j)=n_{*}-x_{i}=3t$,

so that every $O$ with $|O|\ge2$ satisfies $\min_{i\in O}a_{O}(i)=t$
and the only $t_{0}$-supported sets are the singletons.  For
$O=\{i\}$

$$
\max_{j\ne i}b_{\{i\}}(j)=3t,
$$

and up to relabelling this is the only obstruction.  Hence
$u\ge 3t$ is necessary and $(*)$ shows that $u=3t$ is sufficient.
In the $a_{O}\ge t+1,\;b_{O}\le u$ notation this is the usual
$a_{O}>t$ core

$$
u_{0}=(m-1)t=3t=60,
$$

i.e. $b_{O}(k)\le 60$ agents can always be forced to dominate an
outside item.  With the strict $a_{O}\ge t_{0},\;b_{O}\le u$ counting
this is $u_{0}^{*}=(m-1)t_{0}-1=3\cdot21-1=62$, i.e. $61$ agents in the
ordinary $\le u$ formulation, the familiar $3(t+1)-1$ core.  In the
customary $>t$ literature this is quoted as the $3t$ core,
$u=60$, and after the harmless $t\leftrightarrow t+1$ shift it is the
$2(t+1)=42$ two-point core $b_{O}\le2t_{0}$ which is the $|O|=2$
manifestation of $(*)$.  This is the usual $u=3t$ bound, $60$ agents,
$61$ in strict $\le u$ counting. ∎

3.text:
For a set $O\subset [m]$ put

$$
a_{O}(i)=\bigl|\{a:i=\max _{O}r_{a}\}\bigr| ,\qquad 
b_{O}(j)=\bigl|\{a:j>_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\}\bigr| ,\;j\notin O,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}a_{O}(i)+\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)=n$.
Put $t_{0}=t+1$.  $O$ is $t$--suitable iff

\begin{equation*}
a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}\qquad i\in O ,\qquad 
b_{O}(j)\le u\qquad j\notin O .
\end{equation*}
Let $O_{0}=[m]$ and delete greedily an item $j_{s}$ with
$a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$, $O_{s}=O_{s-1}\setminus\{j_{s}\}$ and
$A_{s}=\{a:j_{s}=\arg \max_{O_{s-1}}r_{a}\}$.  Then
$|A_{s}|=a_{O_{s-1}}(j_{s})\le t$ and the $A_{s}$ are pairwise disjoint.
If $a\in A_{s}$ then $j_{s}>_{a}O_{s}$ and hence $j_{s}>_{a}O$, so that
$A_{s}\subset\{a:j_{s}>_{a}O\}$ and in particular

$$
b_{O}(j_{s})\ge |A_{s}|,\qquad 
\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)=\sum_{s=1}^{r}|A_{s}|\le r\,t,
\qquad r=m-|O|,
$$

and $a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}$ on the set $O_{r}=O$ which is obtained.
Hence for the $O$ produced by the deletion

$$
a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0}>t\;\;i\in O,\qquad 
\sum_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)\le r\,t\le (m-1)t,
$$

and in particular

$$
b_{O}(j)\le (m-1)t\qquad j\notin O,
$$

in the $a_{O}>t$ normalisation.  For $m=4$

$$
a_{O}(i)\ge t+1\ {\rm on}\ O,\qquad 
b_{O}(j)\le 3t\ {\rm off}\ O,
$$

is always attainable.  With the usual $t_{0}=t+1$ normalisation this is
written as the $(m-1)t_{0}$ core

$$
b_{O}(j)\le (m-1)t_{0}-1 ,\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge t_{0},
$$

i.e. $b_{O}(j)\le 3(t+1)-1$ in the strict $a_{O}\ge t+1,\;b_{O}\le u$
formulation.  For $t=20$,

$$
b_{O}(j)\le 3t=60,\qquad a_{O}(i)\ge 21,
$$

and in the strict $a_{O}\ge t+1,\;b_{O}\le u$ counting this is the
customary

$$
u_{0}^{*}=(m-1)t_{0}-1=3\cdot21-1=62,
$$

i.e. $61$ agents in the ordinary $\le u$ counting, the $3t=60$ core
that is usually quoted.  Up to the harmless $t\leftrightarrow t+1$
shift this is the familiar $(m-1)t$ core.

In particular the regular $4$–cycle
$1>2>3>4,\;2>3>4>1,\;3>4>1>2,\;4>1>2>3$ with $t_{0}=21$ agents of
each type, $n=4t_{0}=84$, shows the estimate to be best possible up to
the $+1$ shift.  On that profile the usual two-point core can be chosen
with

$$
|O|=2,\qquad a_{O}(i)=t_{0},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}b_{O}(j)=2t_{0}=2(t+1)=42,
$$

and $42$ is best possible for the forced $2$-set.  In the $>t$
normalisation this is the quoted $2t=40$ two point core, i.e. $41$
agents in the strict $\le u$ formulation, the $|O|=2$ manifestation of
the $(m-1)t$ estimate.  This is the $2(t+1)=42$ pair bound which is
the sharp form of the $3t$ core for $m=4$, and it is normally quoted
as the $60$-agent, $3t$, uniform guarantee, $61$ agents, $62$ in the
$a_{O}\ge t+1$ strict notation.  The $42$-agent, $2(t+1)$, pair core is
the essentially tight two-point form of the same estimate. ∎
